exp.6:11:
When they go off seeking help from other nations, I will throw my net over them, the way one catches birds, and bring them down. I will punish them according to what was already declared to them in their assemblies.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, like a naive dove, ran from Egypt to Assyria looking for protection, instead of returning to God. He had redeemed them, yet they answered him with lies and sought him only for grain and wine. Some understand "what has been heard" as the earlier warnings from God; the text allows other readings.

For today: when pressure comes, let us not run first to everything else. Let us seek God sincerely, not only when we need something.
exp.0:6:
God says he will have mercy on Judah, the southern kingdom, and will save them "by the Lord their God," that is, through Himself. He will not rescue them with weapons or armies. The verse's "save them" is the same phrase as "I will save them," and the horsemen in view are the cavalry of war.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just announced judgment on Israel, the northern kingdom, for its unfaithfulness, and shows it through the name of the daughter, Lo-ruhamah, "not pitied." This verse contrasts with that: Judah will receive compassion. Many connect it with the deliverance of Jerusalem from Assyria in the time of Hezekiah (2 Kings 19), although the text does not say so in those words.

For today: do not place your security only in your resources, your preparation, or your strength. Do your part responsibly, but rest in the fact that salvation and mercy come from God, and return to Him with confidence.
exp.9:11:
God invites his people to sow righteousness and reap mercy, that is, to live uprightly and receive the fruit of faithful love. "Break up your fallow ground" means working hard ground that has long gone uncultivated, in other words, opening a hardened heart. "It is time to seek the Lord" means that the opportunity is now, until he comes and teaches righteousness.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, called Ephraim. The people had trusted in their own strength and their idolatry, and for this judgment was coming. Even so, before the punishment, God offers them a way out: to return to him with humility and sincerity.

Today we can ask ourselves what area of our life has become hardened. With humility, let us set aside time to pray and read the Bible, and begin to practice justice and kindness in some concrete way, without waiting for tomorrow.
exp.6:15:
They turned back, the verse says, but not toward God Most High. They were like a deceitful bow, meaning a bent bow that misses its target even though it looks sound. Their leaders would fall by the sword for speaking with pride and arrogance. The verse says they would be mocked, and the people would laugh at them in Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century B.C., to the northern kingdom. God complains that they were seeking things like grain and new wine, not Him. Although He had strengthened them, they plotted evil. Some understand the reference to Egypt as the place they would go looking for help, or the place where they would be humiliated.

For today: changing direction or doing religious activities is not enough; one must turn to God Himself, with the heart. Examine whether you are seeking Him or only His blessings, and ask Him for sincerity.
exp.3:0:
God calls his people to listen. The word rendered "controversy" here means that God brings them to a kind of legal case, as in a lawsuit, to present his charge against them. The accusation is that there is no truth in the land (faithfulness and honesty), no mercy (steadfast love and compassion), and no knowledge of God (knowing him and living according to his will).

Hosea was a prophet who spoke in the northern kingdom, Israel, in a time of great injustice. God speaks through him. The verses that follow list sins such as lying, stealing, adultery and violence, and warn that the whole land would suffer for them. God does not accuse out of whim; he wants to bring his people back to himself.

For today: consider whether there is truth and compassion in your home and work. Knowing God is not only knowing facts, but reflecting his character in how you speak and treat others.
exp.1:3:
It says that God will not have compassion on this woman's children, because they were born in the midst of a life of unfaithfulness. "Unfaithfulness" is the meaning here, and "compassion" means mercy or forgiveness.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The mother represents Israel, the people who had been unfaithful to him by worshiping idols and trusting in other lovers. The children are the people of that generation, who followed the same path. Many understand this as a severe judgment, but the book goes on to promise restoration: God disciplines to call his people back.

For today: examine the things in which you place your trust in place of God, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Return to him sincerely, for his warnings aim to heal us, not destroy us.
exp.12:10:
God speaks: "I gave you a king when I was angry, and I took him away when I was furious." The words "díte" and "quitélo" are old forms of "I gave" and "I took away," so those sentences are removed.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim). He reminds them that they asked for a human king to feel secure (1 Samuel 8). Now, in the midst of their fall, no king can save them. Some understand that the king given in anger refers to Saul; others think it refers to the kings of the northern kingdom in general. The text does not specify.

For today: before asking God for what we desire so insistently, let us ask ourselves whether we trust in Him or in something that gives us security. Let us seek His will, because only in Him is our true help.
exp.8:16:
He says God will reject them, that is, set them aside, because they did not listen to him. The sense of "reject" here is to cast away or throw out. "Listen" in this verse means to obey, not merely to hear. As a result, they will wander without direction, from one place to another, among the nations (the word for nations here refers to foreign peoples).

The prophet Hosea speaks, acting as God's messenger, announcing judgment on Israel, also called Ephraim. Gilgal was a place where the people had fallen into deep wickedness. God charges that, despite his warnings, they went on their own way. Many understand this to announce the exile under Assyria, although the text gives no further detail.

For today: hearing God is more than listening to a message; it is obeying him. Today you can choose one thing God has shown you in his Word and put it into practice with humility, trusting in his mercy.
exp.1:19:
God says that he himself promises to marry his people again, and he will do it "in faithfulness," that is, with firm loyalty and commitment. The result is that they will "know the Lord." Here "know" does not mean only knowing facts, but having a close and personal relationship. To "betroth" means to make a commitment to marriage.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, seeking other gods, and God had disciplined them. Even so, he promises to restore them. The verses before this one speak of peace, security, and a commitment forever, with justice, mercy, and tenderness.

For today: God does not give up on someone who walks away; his faithfulness is stronger than our failures. Today you can return to him with confidence and seek to know him better each day, speaking with him in prayer and reading his Word.
exp.8:7:
It says that Ephraim, that is the northern kingdom of Israel, was supposed to be like a watchman standing guard for his God. But the prophet whom God sends finds traps on every road he travels, and hostility even inside the house of God. A watchtower is a tower or lookout post.

The prophet Hosea speaks, roughly 750 to 725 years before Christ, when Israel had sunk into idolatry and injustice. Some understand that Ephraim was meant to keep watch together with the prophet; others, that Ephraim spied on the prophet with bad intent. In both cases, the people rejected the voice of God.

Today, ask yourself whether you listen with humility to someone who corrects you with truth, or whether you treat them as an enemy. A biblical and loving correction can be a gift from God.
exp.0:1:
It says God began to speak through Hosea and commanded him to marry a woman of unfaithful, sexually immoral conduct, that is, a woman of whoredoms, and to have children with her. The words "whoredoms" and "whore" are used here also as an image of spiritual unfaithfulness: turning one's back on God to follow other gods.

The Lord speaks, and the message is addressed to the kingdom of Israel, which had filled itself with idolatry. God uses Hosea's life as a visible sign: just as that woman would be unfaithful to her husband, the people had been unfaithful to God. Scholars disagree about whether the scene was literal or symbolic, and about whether Gomer was already unfaithful before the marriage or became so afterward.

For today: God calls us to a loyalty of the heart, not merely to keeping up religion. Ask yourself what things occupy the place that belongs to God, and return to Him with confidence.
exp.8:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel, here called Ephraim, will lose their place in the land God gave them. They will be taken back to Egypt and to Assyria, and there they will eat food that is unclean, that is, impure according to the law of Moses. "Unclean things" is the word for food, and "Ephraim" is the main tribe of the northern kingdom.

The one speaking is the prophet Hosea, announcing God's message. Israel had turned away from God to worship idols and to trust in the harvests and in their profits. Hosea warns that there will be consequences, and exile is the most serious of them. Some understand "return to Egypt" literally, and others understand it as an image of returning to slavery.

For today: check in what you trust most, whether in God or in your income and achievements. God calls us to return to Him with sincerity, before other things pull us away from His presence.
exp.1:21:
There is said to be a chain of answers: God answers the heavens, the heavens answer the earth, and the earth answers with grain, wine, and oil, the basic foods of the people. In the end, all that fruit "answers" Jezreel. Jezreel means "God sows."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, and because of that there was punishment. But here God promises to restore the relationship, like a husband who takes his wife back. Jezreel, which once sounded like judgment, now becomes an image of blessing and sowing. Scholars interpret it in several ways, but all see a promise of renewal.

For today: when you feel your life is dry because of your failures, remember that God can restore. Return to him with confidence, and wait for his provision step by step.
exp.0:10:
God promises that Judah and Israel, two divided peoples, will come back together. They will appoint one leader (the "head") and they will "come up out of the land." This may mean they will come out of exile, or that they will spring up like a sown crop, since Jezreel means "God sows." The day of Jezreel will be great: a day of restoration.

Hosea writes to a northern kingdom that has been unfaithful to God. The names of his children, such as Lo-ammi ("not my people"), announced judgment. But God, who is speaking, adds hope: rejection will not be his final word. Some Christians see in that "head" a reference to Christ; others think first of a king from the line of David.

For today: if you feel far from God or divided from others, remember that God knows how to gather and heal. Ask him today to help you take one concrete step toward reconciliation.
exp.11:3:
This verse says that Jacob, while still in his mother's womb, grabbed his brother Esau by the heel. It also says that, as an adult, through his strength he wrestled with an angel and prevailed.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people sought safety in alliances with Assyria and Egypt, and not in God. Hosea reminds them of the story of their ancestor Jacob: a cunning man who, in the end, wept and begged God for mercy. Some think this is a call to repentance; others think it also points out Jacob's faults.

When you feel weak or afraid, do not trust your own plans. Cling to God in prayer, even with tears, and wait for his blessing.
exp.7:4:
God says that the calf of Samaria, an idol, is something He rejects. The phrase "my anger burned" means "my anger was kindled." The phrase "attain to innocency" means becoming clean. The Hebrew text can be understood in two ways: that the calf drew them away from God, or that God rejected the calf. In both cases, the idol separates them from Him.

Hosea speaks to Israel, the northern kingdom, whose center was Samaria. God accuses them of setting up kings without consulting Him and of making idols out of their silver and gold. The calves recall the worship that Jeroboam established at Bethel and Dan. God warns that this path ends in ruin.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting in God's place: money, success, or security. Give it to Him sincerely, and ask Him to cleanse you and guide you.
exp.7:9:
Verse 10 says that even though Israel pays other nations to become its allies, God himself will gather them, that is, bring them against Israel. Israel will suffer for a little while under the weight of the tribute demanded by the king and the princes. The words "hired among the nations" mean paying or contracting; the "nations" are the peoples around them; "sorrow" means suffering under oppression.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, also called Ephraim, sought political protection in Assyria and paid for alliances instead of trusting God. Many understand "gather" as a reference to judgment: those same powers would turn against them. The text does not spell out all the historical details.

For today: when you are afraid, do not buy security with things that pull you away from God. Pray first, seek wise counsel, and trust that He cares for you better than any human alliance.
exp.1:22:
God promises to plant his people in the land like a seed that he himself tends. He says he will have mercy on the one who had not received mercy, and he will say to those who were not his people, "You are my people." Then they will answer, "You are my God."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from him through idolatry. The names of Hosea's children announced judgment, and here restoration is announced. After the discipline, God promises to begin again with his people.

For today: if you feel that you have failed or that you are far from God, remember that his mercy can change your story. Return to him with sincerity and say to him with confidence, "You are my God."
exp.6:4:
It says that on the feast day of the king, the leaders of the land became so drunk on wine that the king ended up sick from it. Furthermore, the king joined himself with "scorners," that is, mocking people who make fun of what is sacred. "Made him sick" can also be understood as having warmed him, or inflamed him, through the wine.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom of Israel. He denounces that its rulers lived in corruption, deceit, and excess, and that no one sought God. Scholars debate exactly which feast or king is meant, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: let us be careful about whom we keep company with and what things control us. Bad company and excess cloud our judgment and pull us away from God. Let us ask Him for wisdom and seek friends who encourage us to do what is right.
exp.10:2:
God says that he taught Ephraim, that is, Israel, to walk, like a father who holds his little child by the arms so that he can take his first steps. The phrase "taking them by their arms" shows how close and gentle that care was. But they did not realize that it was God who was looking after them and healing them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He recalls how he loved Israel from the time he brought them out of Egypt, when they were like a child. Yet the people turned away after the Baals, false gods. The passage shows the pain of a father who cared for them tenderly and received no gratitude in return.

For today: we often receive help, protection and strength without noticing that they come from God. Today you can pause for a moment, remember how He has sustained you in the past, and give Him thanks sincerely.
exp.6:9:
It says that Israel's pride stands up as a witness that accuses him to his face. Although hard things happened to them, they did not return to the Lord their God, nor did they seek him. The phrase about "they turned" is rendered in the verse as "do not return," and the phrase meaning "in spite of all this" appears in the verse as "for all this."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people were weakened: foreign powers were wearing them down, and they did not even notice. Instead of repenting, they sought help from Egypt and Assyria. God denounces their stubbornness and their spiritual blindness.

For today: pride can keep us from seeing our problems. When something in your life is wearing away, do not look first for human solutions. Humble yourself, return to God, and ask him to show you the truth with sincerity.
exp.3:11:
They consult a piece of wood, an idol, or a stick, as if it could give them answers. The words "stock" and "staff" both refer to wooden objects. "Whoredoms" here refers to spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to follow other gods. That spirit deceived them, and they turned away from their God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. He accuses them of having stopped attending to the LORD and of practicing idolatrous worship on the mountains, under leafy trees. Some scholars think there were also sexual practices tied to those cults, although the details are debated.

Today we can look for answers in things that have no life or truth: horoscopes, fashions, or money. Better to seek God in prayer and in his Word, where there is sure guidance.
exp.12:2:
It says that Israel, because it has abandoned God, will soon disappear. It uses four images of things that pass away: the morning mist, the early dew that the sun dries up, the chaff that the wind carries off when grain is threshed, and the smoke that rises out of the smokehouse opening. The smoke image is explained as referring to an opening or window through which smoke goes out.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, the most important tribe of the northern kingdom, had been respected, but it fell into the worship of Baal. Now they were making silver idols and even kissing calves. God warns that what seemed strong will have no future without Him. Right after, He reminds them that only He saved them from Egypt.

For today: everything we put in place of God, such as money, fame, or security, fades away like smoke. Today you can ask yourself what you are resting your life on, and trust God again, the only One who endures.
exp.12:12:
It says that pains like those of a woman giving birth will come upon Ephraim. But the problem is that he is a son without wisdom: instead of coming out at the right time, he stays stuck at the moment of birth, at the point where he should be born. The word "unwise" here refers to a foolish person who does not understand what he should do.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. He rebukes them for their sin and their stubbornness, since they did not repent in time. The image of birth shows that there was a chance to move forward, but they resisted. Some scholars see judgment here; others also see a call to return.

Today, we should not delay repentance. If God shows us a mistake, it is wise to respond quickly and with humility, because he wants to give us new life and not leave us stuck.
exp.9:12:
It says that Israel sowed wickedness and therefore reaps deception. The images of the field show that what a person plants is what they harvest. Plowing wickedness and reaping iniquity are farming images. The fruit of lies is a harvest that promises much and gives nothing. The people trusted in their own way and in their many mighty men, not in God.

The passage presents God speaking through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. Earlier, God had invited them to sow righteousness and to seek the Lord. But they preferred injustice, idols, and military strength. For this reason the following text announces the destruction of their fortresses.

For today: examine where your security rests. Every decision is a seed. If you trust only in your money, your strength, or your plans, the harvest will disappoint. Sow justice and mercy, and seek God first.
exp.9:10:
Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, is compared to a well-trained heifer that loves to thresh grain, an easy job that let her eat as she walked. But God says that he will pass over her "fair neck," that is, her strong and well-kept neck, and will put a yoke on her. Then Judah will plow and Jacob will break up the clods, hard labor in the field.

It is God speaking, through the prophet Hosea. Israel had lived at ease and trusted in its own strength, but it had turned away from God for a long time. The yoke announces discipline and the loss of freedom. Some understand that "Judah" and "Jacob" also show that the whole people would be reached; the text allows several readings.

For today: spiritual comfort can make us drowsy. Examine where you have stopped obeying God because you feel settled, and seek him again today, before life demands it of you by force.
exp.12:14:
It says that Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, seems to be prospering among its brothers, the other tribes. But God will send an east wind, a dry and scorching wind that comes from the desert. That wind will dry up its springs and its wells. Then an enemy will plunder the treasure, that is, all the valuable objects of the land. The words for spring and fountain both refer to a source of water.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him through idolatry and political alliances. Most readers understand the wind to represent the invasion of Assyria, although the text presents it as both a real wind and a symbol. The following verse announces the fall of Samaria, its capital.

For today: prosperity is not proof that all is well with God. Examine your heart, and do not trust in your achievements, but in the Lord, who is the fountain that never runs dry.
exp.9:6:
It says that the king of Samaria will be taken away or destroyed suddenly, and that he will vanish like the foam that floats on the water: he seems to be something, but a wave carries him off without leaving a trace. Some translators understand the word as "foam," and others as "twig" or "splinter"; the Hebrew allows both ideas, and both speak of something fragile.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel, whose capital was Samaria. The people trusted in their kings and in the golden calves of Beth-aven (Bethel), a false worship. God announces that neither the throne nor the idols will be able to save them, and that Assyria will subdue them.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our security: in power, money, or leaders, who pass away like foam. Only God is firm. Let us trust first in Him.
exp.7:10:
It says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, filled the land with altars. They were supposed to serve for offering sacrifices and asking God for forgiveness, but they became a source of sin. It is as if God were saying: "So many altars, and all of them ended up being a place to sin."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel sought security in alliances with powers like Assyria, instead of trusting in God. It also practiced a religion full of rituals, but without obedience. That is why God rebukes them and announces that they will bear the consequences.

We can have a great deal of religious activity and still have our hearts far from God. Today it is good to ask ourselves whether our prayers, songs and service come from sincere obedience, or whether they are only a custom that calms the conscience. God seeks a faithful heart.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the people are to call their brothers "Ammi," which means "my people," and their sisters "Ruhamah," which means "pitied" or "one who has obtained mercy." The words "say" and "unto" are older forms of the modern "say" and "to." These names reverse the earlier message.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom. Earlier, the children had been given names of rejection: "Not my people" and "Not pitied." Now God announces that he will again call them his own. Some understand this as foreshadowing restoration after the punishment. The New Testament cites this idea to speak of grace that reaches everyone (Romans 9:25-26; 1 Peter 2:10).

For today: if you feel far from God because of your failures, remember that his mercy can change your story. And encourage others to believe that God still calls them his own.
exp.1:6:
It says that Israel, portrayed as an unfaithful wife, will run after her lovers (the idols and the allied nations), but she will not be able to catch them or find them. Then she will say: "I will go and return to my first husband, for then it was better with me than now." The phrase "I will return" in this verse is rendered in the King James wording as "I will go and return," and "she shall seek them" refers to her searching for her lovers.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. His people had left him to worship Baal, believing that the idols gave them bread, wool and oil. God blocks their paths with thorns, not only to punish, but so that she will recognize where all good things come from. Many see here a first step toward repentance, although her motive still seems self-interested.

Today we might ask ourselves: in what things do I seek security apart from God? When those things fail, it is not the end, but an invitation to return to Him, who always welcomes the one who comes back.
exp.6:12:
God says "Woe to them!" with grief, not only with anger. The people turned away from him and rebelled. "Destruction" speaks of ruin as the consequence. "I redeemed them" means God rescued them, as when he brought them out of Egypt. Even so, they spoke lies against him, that is, they dealt with him falsely and did not keep what they said about him.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. Israel, like a naive dove, was seeking help in Egypt and in Assyria, and not in God. So the Lord announces that he will catch them like birds in a net. Many understand that their lies include a religion without heart, as the following verse says.

For today: do not seek security only in human resources while ignoring God. Remember what he has done for you and cry out to him sincerely, not only when you need grain and new wine.
exp.11:12:
Here Jacob, the ancestor of Israel, had to flee to the land of Aram, which was the region of Syria and Mesopotamia. There he worked for another man in exchange for a wife, and for her he tended sheep.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim, which had turned away from Him. He reminds them of their humble origin: their father Jacob was a fugitive and a servant. Then the text contrasts this with what God did afterward: He brought Israel out of Egypt through a prophet, Moses, and cared for them. Interpreters disagree about the exact tone, but the contrast seems clear: Israel was to remember its smallness and the faithfulness of God.

For today: remembering where God brought us from helps us live with gratitude rather than pride. Today you can thank Him for a difficult season in which He sustained you.
exp.1:7:
God says that Israel, whom he addresses as "she," did not realize that it was he who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, that is, the basic food of each day. He also gave her plenty of silver and gold, but with that gold they made an idol of Baal. "They made to Baal" means they used it to craft images of that god.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who seeks other lovers, that is, the idols. She thinks they are the ones who give her prosperity. For this reason God blocks her path, so that she will wake up and return to him.

For today: what we have, whether work, food, or money, comes from the hand of God. Before using it, give thanks. Ask yourself whether you are using it to honor him or whether it has become your main security.
exp.1:11:
He says God will destroy Israel's vines and fig trees. She said these were her wages, the payment her lovers had given her. God will turn them into a thicket, a wild tangle of undergrowth, and the wild animals will eat what is left.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel is described as an unfaithful wife who credited her harvests to the Baal gods and not to the Lord. This judgment is a strong discipline. But the following context shows the goal: God will lead her into the wilderness and speak to her heart.

For today: ask yourself where you think what you have comes from. Thank God for your work, your food and your family, and do not put your security in things that can disappear. He corrects in order to restore.
exp.8:6:
It says that the time has come when God punishes. "Visitation" here means a moment when God steps in to judge, and "recompense" is receiving what is deserved. Israel is going to recognize it. They call the prophet a "fool" and the spiritual man "mad," and this is because of the great wickedness of the people and their strong hostility.

Hosea, a prophet of God, speaks to the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), which lived in idolatry and injustice. Scholars debate whether the insults are spoken by the people mocking the prophet, or whether Hosea quotes them with irony. Either way, the people rejected the warning, and the exile was drawing near.

For today: when someone corrects us with truth, let us not dismiss it with mockery or anger. Better to ask humbly whether God is speaking to us, and to change in time.
exp.7:11:
God says that he wrote to Israel the great and valuable things of his law, but the people treated them as if they were something strange, belonging to someone else, of no importance to them.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people filled the land with altars and sacrifices, yet they ignored what God had already taught them. Their religion was all outward appearance, without obedience. That is why God announces that he will remember their sin.

For today: it is not enough to have a Bible at home or to practice religious customs. Ask God to help you read his Word as something of your own, near and precious, and decide today to obey one specific thing it teaches you.
exp.3:4:
It says that God's judgment will reach everyone: the priest will fall "in the day," the prophet "in the night," and also the "mother," who represents the nation. "Destroy" means to wipe out completely, the way a tree is cut down at the root. "Fall" speaks of ruin, not of a simple stumble.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the priest and the people of northern Israel. There was lying, violence and idolatry, and the leaders were not teaching the law. Some think that "day" and "night" show that no one will escape; others think the fall will be total. The text does not fully settle this.

For today: Those who teach or guide others carry a great responsibility before God. And each of us can ask whether we are truly seeking his Word, because without it we lose our way.
exp.13:3:
God promises to heal the backsliding of his people. "I will heal" is the meaning of the word that is sometimes rendered "medicine," and "their backsliding" is their tendency to turn away from God. The phrase about loving them is rendered here as "I will love them of my own free will, freely, without their deserving it." The phrase "mine anger is turned away" means that his anger has already passed.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from him, trusting in Assyria, in their war horses, and in their idols. But God invites them to return with sincere words of repentance, and here he answers with a promise of forgiveness and restoration.

For today: when you fail or have wandered away from God, do not hide yourself or try to fix it alone. Return to him with honesty, confess your fault, and receive his forgiveness. God does not only forgive; he also heals the depths of the heart and loves you generously.
exp.8:15:
Hosea says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, has been struck like a tree that is wounded. Its root has dried up, and it will no longer bear fruit. The root is the base of the plant that holds it up and feeds it. Even if they have children, God will take the life of the beloved children of their womb.

The prophet Hosea speaks here, announcing God's judgment. The people had abandoned God through idolatry and injustice, and Gilgal is mentioned as a place of their wickedness. Some think the sentence before this is from the prophet, and others think it expresses the voice of God; the text does not fully make this clear. The punishment is harsh, but it aims to show how serious it is to ignore God.

For today: let us not allow religious habit to harden our hearts. If God corrects us through his Word, let us listen quickly and return to him, because a life without obedience ends up dry, even when it looks strong on the outside.
exp.11:11:
It says that Gilead is full of wickedness and that everything they do is vanity, that is, something empty. In Gilgal they offered bulls as sacrifices, but their altars will end up like heaps of stones in the furrows of a plowed field. The question "Is Gilead iniquity?" can be understood in several ways, and scholars translate it in different ways.

The passage records God speaking through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel (Ephraim). He had already reminded them that he brought them out of Egypt and sent them prophets. Gilead and Gilgal were places of worship, and it seems that there religion had become empty, mixed with idols and without sincere obedience.

For today: performing religious acts is not enough if the heart is far from God. Ask yourself whether your faith shows in the way you live, in justice and in obedience, and not only in what you do on Sundays.
exp.1:9:
God says that now he is going to expose Israel's "folly," that is, her shameful and senseless conduct, in the sight of her "lovers," the false gods and the nations she trusted in. No one will be able to rescue her from his hand. The word "deliver" means to rescue or save.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, compared to an unfaithful wife. She credited her harvests and wealth to Baal, a Canaanite god, without recognizing that everything came from the Lord. For this reason God announces judgment. Many understand that his goal is to correct her and bring her back to himself, as is seen later in the book.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we are putting in God's place: money, success, or comfort. Let us give thanks to him for what we have, because every good gift comes from his hand.
exp.9:2:
It says that a time will come when the people of Israel will recognize that they have been left without a king. And it admits the reason: they did not fear the Lord, that is, they did not honor or obey him. Then, in discouragement, they ask what a king could possibly do for them. "Fear" here means honoring and revering God.

The prophet Hosea is speaking, delivering God's message to the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier, they were described as a vine that flourished, but they used their blessings to raise altars and idols. Hosea announces that judgment is coming, and that neither the king nor politics will be able to save them. Scholars understand this as a announcement of the fall of the northern monarchy.

For today: no leader, plan, or system can give us what comes only from a life surrendered to God. Ask him to order your heart before anything else.
exp.8:13:
Here the prophet Hosea asks God to give Israel what they deserve. He asks for "a miscarrying womb," a womb that loses the child before birth, and "dry breasts," breasts without milk. These are harsh words: the blessing of having children will be taken away from them.

Hosea speaks to Ephraim, the name of the northern kingdom, Israel. They had fallen into idolatry, and the text mentions Gilgal as a place of their wickedness. Children were a sign of blessing, so losing them was a very painful judgment. Some think Hosea says this with grief, not with pleasure, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he also does so with pain. Let us examine whether we are letting something take the place of God, and return to him with humility while there is still time.
exp.12:5:
It says the people ate until they were full, and that once they were satisfied they became proud. That is why they forgot God. "Pasture" refers to the fields where livestock feed; here it suggests the blessings God gave them. "Filled" means eating until one is satisfied. "Exalted" means becoming full of pride.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. He reminds them that He cared for them in the wilderness and that He alone is their Savior. But when they had abundance, they stopped depending on Him. The verses that follow announce a severe judgment, with images of wild beasts, as the consequence of that forgetfulness.

For today: when everything is going well, it is easy to feel that we do not need God. We can thank Him every day for what we have and remember that everything comes from His hand, so that abundance does not make us proud or forgetful.
exp.1:15:
What the passage says: God promises that a day will come when his people will call him "Ishi," meaning "my husband," with affection and closeness. They will no longer call him "Baali," a name that was also used for a master or lord, but which was the name of the Canaanite god Baal.

Context: The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had gone after the Baals, like an unfaithful wife. Even so, God promises to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her heart, and restore the relationship. Scholars understand the wilderness as a time of starting over, though not all interpret it the same way.

For today: God does not seek only cold obedience, but a relationship of trust and love. Ask yourself whether anything occupies in your heart the place that belongs to God. If you have drifted away, he invites you to return and speak to him with sincerity.
exp.11:0:
Ephraim, the northern kingdom, and the whole house of Israel surrounded God with lies and deceit. The verb "surrounded" is what is meant here. Judah, by contrast, still rules alongside God and is faithful. This last phrase is hard to translate. Some versions say that Judah walks with God, or that it is still loyal. There is also debate about whether the reference to the holy ones means God himself or his faithful people.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel claimed to worship him, but it sought security in alliances with Assyria and Egypt and lived in falsehood. God confronts them with sorrow. Judah fares better for now, though the text that follows shows that God also has a case against her.

Today we might ask whether we are sincere with God or only go through the motions outwardly. Trusting him with honesty is worth more than leaning on our own plans.
exp.4:1:
It says that the people, in offering sacrifices, sank very deep into their sin. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some versions speak of slaughter or of deep rebellion. That is why God says that He will be the rebuker of them all: that is, the one who disciplines and punishes them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He addresses the priests, the people, and the royal household in the northern kingdom. He accuses them of having been a snare and a net at Mizpah and Tabor, probably for leading others toward false worship, though it is not known with precision how.

For today: those who teach or lead others have a great responsibility. If you notice that you are drifting away from God, do not keep sinking: listen quickly to His correction, which seeks to bring you back to Him.
exp.6:7:
It says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, mixed itself with the neighboring nations. It also compares him to a cake that was not turned over: one side was burned and the other side was raw, so it is no good to eat.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was seeking alliances with other nations and copying their customs, instead of trusting the Lord. Meanwhile, the nation was growing weaker, and it did not even notice, as the verses that follow say.

For today: when we mix our faith with everything around us, we are left half-done, without maturing. We can ask God to show us where we are divided and to turn back to Him with our whole heart.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel (called here Ephraim) would not return to Egypt, but that Assyria, another foreign power, would be their king. The reason is clear: they refused to change course, that is, they refused to turn back to God.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Hosea. Before this, God recalls how he cared for Israel like a father who teaches his child to walk, leading them with bands of love. Even so, the people did not recognize his care. Many understand that Egypt represents a return to slavery, and that Assyria was the empire that ended up dominating them. God speaks with pain, not with coldness.

For today: when God corrects us, it is not to destroy us, but to call us back to himself. Today we can ask ourselves: in what area am I ignoring his care? Answering with humility keeps other things from ending up ruling our lives.
exp.10:7:
Here God asks himself: "How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?" Admah and Zeboim were cities destroyed along with Sodom, and God says he cannot treat them that way. "My heart turns within me" and "my compassion is kindled" mean that his compassion stirs with great force inside him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim is another name for the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had rebelled, and punishment was approaching. Even so, God shows a tension between his justice and his love, and in the end his compassion has the final word.

For today: if you have failed, do not run from God thinking he has already rejected you. His discipline does not come from contempt but from a love that does not let you go. Return to him sincerely and trust in his mercy.
exp.12:8:
The verse reads: "O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself; but in me is thine help." The phrase "thou hast destroyed thyself" means that Israel brought ruin upon itself through its own choices. Even so, God leaves a door open: the only true help comes from Him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom, which had turned away from Him to follow idols and to trust in human kings. Earlier, God had described His judgment with fierce images of wild beasts. Afterward He asks where the king is in whom they trusted. Some interpreters read that question as a rebuke, and others as a promise of help despite the punishment.

For today: when your mistakes have left you with no way out, do not blame others or sink into despair. Acknowledge your responsibility and return to God, who continues to offer His help to anyone who asks for it.
exp.5:10:
Judah is also said to have something "planted," or set in place, and that comes when God restores his people. The Hebrew word is usually rendered "harvest," so many versions read: "Also, O Judah, a harvest is set for you." The phrase "returned the captivity" means giving the people back their well-being.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just denounced the wickedness of Israel: violent priests, idolatry, and unfaithfulness. Now he includes Judah, the southern kingdom. There is debate over whether this harvest is one of judgment, because of their sins, or one of blessing, after restoration. Perhaps there is a bit of both.

For today: what we sow through our choices bears fruit sooner or later. But God, who corrects, also restores those who return to him. Today you can sow obedience and trust in him.
exp.0:2:
Hosea obeys what God commanded him: he marries Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim, she becomes pregnant, and she gives him a son. Some older words in the original are rendered in ways that do not appear in your verse, so we will simply describe them: the verb for "went" and "took" in the earlier wording are the same actions shown in the King James text, and the word for giving birth means the same as "bare," which your verse uses.

God had asked Hosea to take a woman who would be unfaithful, and his family would serve as a sign to Israel, which was turning away from God to follow other gods. Scholars discuss whether Gomer was already unfaithful or would become so later, and whether everything happened literally or as a vision. The text does not make this clear. What is clear is that Hosea obeyed.

God sometimes asks us to obey even when we do not understand the whole plan. We can trust that He is faithful and has a purpose. Today, ask yourself: what simple step of obedience has God shown me that I have been putting off? Take it today with confidence.
exp.13:4:
God promises that He Himself will be like the dew to Israel. In dry lands, dew refreshes and gives life during the night. Thanks to that care, the people will blossom like a lily and spread their roots like the cedars of Lebanon, that is, they will grow with strength and stability.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him to trust in Assyria, in war horses, and in idols. But now the people repent, and God responds with forgiveness and healing: He says He will heal their rebellion and love them freely.

When we return to God, He not only forgives but also renews and strengthens us. We can stop looking for security in things that fail and receive from Him new life and deep roots.
exp.5:1:
He says that God, who wounded his people, will also heal them. The phrase meaning "will give us life" is simply rendered here as "will give us life," so no word needs explaining. The expression about a brief span of time, "after two days... on the third day," indicates a short interval before God raises them up. They hope to live again in his presence.

The speakers are the Israelites who say, "Come, let us return to the LORD." However, the next verse shows that God regards their love as fragile, like the morning cloud or the dew that soon disappears. Some understand this as a shallow repentance; others, as a sincere hope. Christians often see here a shadow of the resurrection of Christ, although the text does not say so directly.

Today, we can trust that God restores. But our turning back to him should be constant, not just a passing impulse.
exp.6:6:
The whole people is set on fire like an oven, full of passions and schemes. In their rage they destroyed their own rulers, and one after another their kings fell. The saddest part is that, in the middle of so much crisis, no one calls out to God. The comment about "devoured" and "unto me" has been adapted to the verse above: the word "devoured" means they consumed their judges, and the phrase "unto me" is simply the old way of saying "to me."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. There were conspiracies, drunkenness, and political murders. God complains that, even with so much chaos, the people do not turn back to seek him.

For today: when everything falls into disorder in our lives or around us, let us not trust only in human solutions. Before acting out of anger or ambition, let us pause and call out to God sincerely. He remains attentive to those who seek him.
exp.4:13:
Here God says that he will be like a lion to Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and like a young lion to Judah (the southern kingdom). The phrase translated as "tear" means that he will attack and carry off the prey; the phrase translated as "go away" means that he will leave afterward; and the phrase translated as "take away" means that no one will be able to rescue them from his hand.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The two kingdoms had abandoned God and sought help from Assyria and its king, instead of seeking him. Because of this, God allows judgment. The verses that follow show that he withdraws so that they will recognize their sin and seek him. Some understand this as the Assyrian invasions; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when things become difficult, do not run first to human solutions. If God corrects you, remember that his aim is to bring you back to himself, and you can return today with sincerity.
exp.12:1:
The verse says that they sin more and more. They made for themselves molten images from their silver, idols made according to their own understanding, all of it the work of the craftsmen. Of them they say, "Let the men who sacrifice kiss the calves." This verse says that the people of Israel kept on sinning. With their silver they made statues of molten metal, idols shaped to their liking by craftsmen. Moreover, to those who offered sacrifices they said: "Let the men who sacrifice kiss the calves," that is, worship those images. "According to their own understanding" means according to their own idea. "The craftsmen" are the artisans.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, had once been respected, but it became corrupted by the worship of Baal. God denounces that, instead of trusting in Him, they made gods with their hands. The verses that follow show that this idolatry would lead them to vanish like the morning mist, and God reminds them that only He is the Savior.

Today we may not kiss statues, but we can place our trust in money, success, or an image of God made to our own measure. Ask yourself: what occupies the place of God in my heart? Surrender it to Him in prayer today and return to trusting in Him.
exp.8:8:
Israel had sunk very deep into wickedness and had become thoroughly corrupted. The prophet compares this to the days of Gibeah, a reminder of a terrible episode. Saying that God "remembers" their wrongdoing means that he does not forget their iniquity, and "visit" means that he will come to call them to account and punish their sin.

The prophet Hosea speaks here, sent by God to the northern kingdom (Ephraim). Gibeah is mentioned in Judges 19, where a dreadful crime took place. Many understand Hosea to show that the people had fallen back into violence and degradation of a similar kind. Interpreters differ on the exact details of the comparison, but the general sense is clear: the sin was deep, and God would respond.

Today we can remember that sin grows when we tolerate it. Let us not wait until we have sunk further; let us confess it soon and return to God, who forgives the one who repents.
exp.11:7:
This verse says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) is like a dishonest merchant. In his hand he holds false scales, that is, weights tampered with to cheat the customer. He also loves to oppress, which means he enjoys abusing and taking advantage of others. Some understand that God compares him to the traders of Canaan.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just called the people to return to Him and to practice mercy and justice. But Ephraim boasts of his wealth and says that no one will find sin in him. God shows him that his prosperity is stained by fraud.

Today, we can examine our own scales: are we honest at work, in our prices, in our accounts and in our payments? Making money is not wrong, but God calls us to do it with truth and to treat others well.
exp.11:8:
Ephraim, which represents the northern kingdom of Israel, boasts of its wealth. It says it became rich through its own effort and that no one can accuse it of wickedness or sin in all it has worked for. "Iniquity" means injustice or wickedness.

God, through the prophet Hosea, speaks to a people who trust in their money. The verse before speaks of false scales and oppression, so Ephraim considers itself innocent while it cheats. God reminds it that He is the one who brought it out of Egypt, and that He had sent prophets to correct it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we measure our honesty only by what we achieve. Being successful does not prove that we act rightly. It is wise to examine with humility how we earn our money, and to thank God for what we have.
exp.10:9:
It says that one day the people of Israel will follow the Lord. God himself will roar like a lion, and not as a threat against them but as a strong call. When they hear his voice, his children will come trembling, that is, astonished, moved, and hurrying, from the west, which in the text may refer to the lands of the sea or distant lands.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just said that his heart is stirred and that he will not completely destroy Ephraim, because he is God and not a man. Although Israel deserved judgment, God promises to bring them back. The roar of a lion is sometimes used for judgment, but here it seems to be a call that gathers.

For today: when you have drifted away from God, do not doubt his mercy. His voice may sound firm, but it seeks to bring you home. Respond quickly, with humility, and walk after him again.
exp.0:5:
This verse tells us that Gomer had another daughter, and God asked Hosea to name her "Lo-ruhamah," which means "Not Pitied" or "No Mercy." God explains that He will no longer have compassion on the kingdom of Israel. The phrase "I will utterly take them away" can also be understood as "I will carry them far away" or "I will by no means forgive them"; translations and scholars vary.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who lived in the northern kingdom, Israel, in a time of idolatry and injustice. The names of his children were living messages for the people. This name warned of a coming judgment. But the next verse shows that God would still have mercy on Judah, and that their salvation would not come by military strength, but by Him.

For today: God's mercy is a gift, not a right we can take for granted. Let us take the opportunity today to turn back to Him sincerely, instead of trusting in our own resources.
exp.8:10:
This verse says that Ephraim's glory, that is, its greatness and blessing, will fly away like a bird. And the loss will not come slowly: it will reach from birth, from the womb, and from conception. In other words, the children, who were a sign of prosperity, will stop being born or will not grow up.

The prophet Hosea speaks on God's behalf to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people had fallen into the idolatry of Baal-peor and had become corrupt. God recalls that at the beginning he saw them as fresh grapes in the desert, but now judgment is coming. Many understand the loss of children to be a direct punishment for their sin.

For today: whatever we value most, whether family, success, or recognition, cannot take the place of God. If we let it, it becomes fragile. Let us put God first and receive his blessings with gratitude.
exp.1:18:
It says God promises to take his people as his bride forever. "Betroth" means to bind oneself in marriage. He will do this "in righteousness" (what is right), "in judgment" (good and fair decisions), "in lovingkindness" (compassion), and "in mercies" (tender compassion, a love that is moved with feeling).

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, which had been unfaithful to him by worshiping the Baals, false gods. Before this verse, God promises to remove those names and to give peace. Hosea himself lived through a painful marriage, which serves as an image of God's faithful love toward a people who had turned away.

For today: if you have failed or feel far from God, he does not offer you a passing relationship or one based on your merits. You can return to him with confidence, receive his forgiveness, and let his love guide your decisions and how you treat others.
exp.8:14:
It says that the wickedness of the people of Israel was openly seen in Gilgal, and that there God came to feel rejection toward them. Because of their evil deeds, he will drive them out of his house (probably the land or the covenant family) and will no longer love them as before. "Rebels" means those who revolt against God. "I will drive them out" is the meaning of the phrase.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim. Gilgal was an important place in its history, but here it is associated with idolatry and sin. It is not known with precision what event is meant; scholars explain it in several ways. God makes this announcement of judgment because the people and their leaders rejected his covenant.

For today: it is not enough to have places, rituals, or religious activities if the heart turns away from God. Ask him to examine your heart, and if there is something that does not please him, return to him with sincerity. His judgment is serious, but it always invites repentance.
exp.3:14:
Hosea 4:15 says that even though Israel, the northern kingdom, has given itself over to spiritual unfaithfulness, Judah, the southern kingdom, should take care not to fall into the same thing. He warns them not to go to Gilgal or up to Beth-aven, places of corrupted worship, and not to swear, "As the Lord lives," while they mix their worship with idols. "Play the harlot" here speaks of unfaithfulness to God; "Beth-aven" means "house of wickedness" and is probably a way of referring to Bethel, "house of God."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea in the eighth century B.C. He accuses Israel of mixing faith with idolatrous rites. He wants to keep Judah from following that same path.

For today: saying religious words is not enough when the heart is divided. Examine which places, habits, or influences pull you away from God, and step away from them before they carry you off. Being sincere with God matters more than looking spiritual.
exp.7:7:
He says Israel will be "swallowed up," that is, devoured or absorbed by other nations. Very soon it will be among the nations like a vessel in which there is no pleasure, a despised pot that no one wants and that gets thrown away. "Soon" is the meaning of the word "presto," and the "nations" are the peoples around them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The northern people, called Israel or Ephraim, had abandoned God: they made a calf to worship in Samaria and sought protection from Assyria instead of trusting the Lord. God announces the consequences of that path. Historians connect this judgment with the fall of Samaria to Assyria, around 722 B.C.

For today: when we look for security in things that are not God, money, power, or alliances, we end up empty. Today you can ask yourself what you truly trust in and return your trust to the Lord, who truly sustains and gives worth to his people.
exp.8:9:
God says that when He found Israel, it was like finding grapes in the middle of the desert: a joyful and refreshing surprise. He saw their ancestors as the first figs on the tree, sweet and eagerly awaited. But then they went to Baal-peor, a place where the false god Baal was worshiped, and they gave themselves over to him. "Went over to shame" means they turned away from God and ended up disgraced. They became "detestable," that is, repugnant, just like the idol they loved.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom (Ephraim). He reminds them of the affection with which He chose them and contrasts it with their unfaithfulness. Baal-peor is mentioned in Numbers 25, when the people fell into idolatry and sin.

For today: what we worship shapes us over time. Let us ask God to help us love what is good and to return to Him, who looks on us with tenderness.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that the Lord, to whom Israel must return, is the God of hosts, that is, the God of all power, and that his name is to be remembered. The name by which God wishes to be remembered and called upon is the name the verse is about. The name is written in an old form that the reader may recognize from older Bibles, but its meaning is the name of God itself.

Hosea speaks in God's name to the people of the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. He reminds them of the story of Jacob, who wrestled with the angel and sought God's blessing at Bethel. Some understand that Hosea presents Jacob as an example of seeking God; others also see a warning in his deceitful character. Then he calls them to return to God.

For today: remember who God is, powerful and faithful, and return to him with humility. Practice justice and mercy in your work and in your dealings with others.
exp.10:8:
God says he will not let the full blaze of his anger fall on Ephraim, which is another name for the northern kingdom, Israel. The verse of the word "execute" and the note about "á" being "a" are not carried over, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees. The reason he gives is: "I am God, and not man." He is the Holy One who is present among his people. The last phrase, "I will not enter into the city," can be understood in different ways: that he will not come as an enemy to destroy it, or that he will not act with human fury.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. His people had rebelled and abandoned him, and yet God shows a heart torn between judgment and compassion. He recalls Admah and Zeboiim, cities that were destroyed, but says he will not do the same to Israel.

For today: when you fail, do not think that God reacts like a wounded and vengeful person. His holiness includes mercy. Return to him with confidence and let his patience move you to change.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel, like Adam, broke the covenant with God. "Transgressed" means stepping over a boundary, disobeying. "Dealt treacherously" means acting with betrayal or disloyalty. "There" seems to point to a specific place, but it is not known which one.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just said that he desires mercy and the knowledge of God, not only offerings. The people kept the rituals, but their hearts were unfaithful. Some translate "like men" as "like Adam" or as a place called Adam; scholars do not agree. Even so, the central idea is clear: they broke their promise to God.

For today: it is not enough to attend church or keep religious customs. God looks for a faithful heart and genuine love. Today you can check whether your relationship with him is sincere, and whether your treatment of others reflects the mercy he has shown you.
exp.13:8:
Says that whoever is wise and prudent must understand what God has said throughout this whole book. The ways of the Lord are right, that is, upright and just. Those who obey, "the just," will walk securely along them. On the other hand, the "rebels," those who oppose God, will stumble and fall on those very same paths.

Hosea closes his book with this reflective statement. Throughout the book, God accused Israel (Ephraim) of idolatry and unfaithfulness, but He also called them to return to Him. Just before, God promises to heal and renew those who repent. This verse is the final invitation to think carefully and choose well.

For today: wisdom is not merely knowing things, but obeying God. Think of one area of your life where you have resisted His guidance, and surrender it to Him today with trust, believing that His way is good.
exp.3:10:
What it says: Hosea says that unfaithfulness, wine, and new wine "take away the heart." New wine is the fresh juice of the grape, still fermenting. "Take away the heart" means that these things rob a person of good judgment, understanding, and loyalty. In other words, these pleasures leave a person without the sense to decide well.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. The people and their priests had turned away from the LORD and mixed in with idolatry and the worship practices of neighboring peoples. God shows that this is not only a moral problem, but that their disordered desires made them blind to recognizing Him.

For today: Examine what things are clouding your mind and pulling you away from God. When something takes away your clarity and your desire to seek Him, set limits and ask God and trusted people for help.
exp.4:5:
They will go with their flocks and their herds, meaning their sacrifices, to seek the Lord, but they will not find him. He has withdrawn himself from them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim) and to Judah. The people had fallen into idolatry, which the text calls spiritual unfaithfulness, and their pride kept them from turning back to God. That is why, although they carried out religious offerings, their hearts remained far from him.

For today: performing rites, attending meetings, or giving offerings is not enough if the heart does not repent. God invites us to seek him with humility and sincerity, leaving behind whatever pulls us away from him. Today you can pray and ask him to show you what you need to change.
exp.4:6:
This verse says that the people were unfaithful to God. "They have dealt treacherously" means betraying or breaking a commitment. "Strange children" may refer to children born from a life far from God, or children of marriages with foreigners or of idolatrous practices; it is interpreted in several ways. "Now shall a month devour them" perhaps speaks of a brief time: ruin will come soon and will carry off them and their lands.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who addresses the northern kingdom (Israel or Ephraim) and also warns Judah. They worshiped idols and yet presented offerings, but God had turned away from them. The warning seeks to make them aware of their sin.

Today: it is not enough to offer things to God if the heart is far from Him. Examine your life with sincerity, leave behind what separates you from God, and return to Him with humility, before sin causes you more harm.
exp.6:1:
God says that the people do not stop to think that he remembers every one of their wrongdoings. The phrase "I keep in memory" means that God does not forget or overlook sin. The phrase "their own doings surround them" means that their evil actions hem them in like a wall, and everything is in plain view before God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, here called Ephraim, and its capital, Samaria, were living in deceit, injustice, and violence. God wanted to heal them, but as he drew near to them, their sin was laid bare. They believed no one could see them, and so they kept on in their wickedness.

For today: do not live as if what is hidden does not matter. God sees everything, but he also offers forgiveness. Tell him honestly today what you have kept silent about, and let him heal your heart.
exp.12:7:
He says that God will come against his people like a she-bear that has lost her cubs: furious and dangerous. The phrase about the chest is an old way of speaking of the breast, the center of life. Then he compares God to a lion that devours, and to wild beasts of the field that tear apart. It is a very strong image of judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. When the people had abundance, they grew proud and forgot their God. For this reason he announces punishment. Interpreters understand that the judgment would come through enemy nations, although here it is described with images of animals. Even so, the following verse leaves a door open: "in me is your help."

For today: when everything goes well for us, it is easy to forget God. Let us ask him for a humble and grateful heart, and let us return to him soon, for his correction seeks to rescue us.
exp.1:16:
It says that God will remove from the mouth of his people the names of the Baals, that is, the false gods they worshiped. After that change, no one will remember them or call on them anymore.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, going after the Baals (Canaanite gods tied to rain and harvest). Hosea uses the image of a broken marriage. Here God promises to restore his people. They used to call him "Baali," which could mean "my lord" or "my Baal," but God wants them to call him "my husband," with affection and faithfulness.

For today: God does not only forgive, he also heals the heart. We can ask ourselves what things have taken God's place in our lives and ask him to help us let them go, so that his name becomes the one we speak most often with love and trust.
exp.9:1:
It says that Israel's heart was divided: they were not fully faithful to God. Because of this, they will now be found guilty. "He" most likely refers to God, who will break down the altars and destroy the sacred images or pillars they used to worship. The word "spoil" in the verse means to plunder or strip away, to leave things in ruin.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. When the land gave them abundance, instead of thanking God, they multiplied altars and idols. They used their blessings to serve themselves and other gods. Some interpreters also see here a reference to the king, but the general sense of the judgment is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves: do the blessings God gives me bring me closer to Him, or do they distract me from Him? A divided heart does not find peace. Ask God to help you love Him with all your heart and to be thankful in abundance.
exp.4:0:
God calls the priests, the people of Israel, and the house of the king to pay close attention, because his judgment is coming upon them. He tells them to "hear ye this," meaning "listen to this," and to "give ye ear," meaning "pay attention." He accuses them of having been a snare, a trap, at Mizpah, and a net spread out on Tabor. Instead of guiding the people, their leaders led them into a fall.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom of Israel. He accuses the religious and political leaders of leading the people into idolatry. Mizpah and Tabor were well-known places, but it is not known with certainty what practices took place there; some think of false worship or deception.

For today: those who have influence, in the church, the family, or the workplace, carry a greater responsibility. Let us ask God that our example helps others draw near to him, not stumble.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Israel's pride is like a witness that accuses them and contradicts them before everyone. Their own arrogance will show that they are wrong. "Ephraim" is the name of the northern kingdom, and their stumbling means they will fall because of their sin. Even Judah, the southern kingdom, will fall along with them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him and worshiped other gods; the Bible calls this unfaithfulness, like the betrayal in a broken marriage. God knows them well and warns them that their pride kept them from returning to Him.

For today: pride keeps us from recognizing our mistakes and returning to God. Ask Him today for humility to admit one specific fault, and take a step to correct it. He welcomes with grace whoever turns to Him with a sincere heart.
exp.11:9:
It says that God is still the same God of Israel who brought them out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom, considered itself rich and innocent, although it used false weights and oppressed others. Scholars interpret this in two ways: as a warning of losing everything and returning to a simple life, or as a promise of restoration. Both ideas fit the passage.

For today: do not trust in your riches or in your own righteousness. Remember that everything you have comes from God, and live with honesty, humility, and gratitude.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that the people of Israel no longer think about returning to God. Their deeds have them trapped. The "thoughts" in the verse are what hold them. The "spirit of whoredoms" speaks of an inner inclination toward spiritual unfaithfulness, that is, worshiping other gods the way a person betrays a spouse. "They have not known the Lord" does not mean they are ignorant of his name, but that they have no real relationship with him. "Turn" means to repent.

Context: The prophet Hosea speaks on God's behalf in the eighth century B.C. Ephraim is another name for the northern kingdom, Israel. God accuses them of idolatry and warns that their hearts have grown hard. Hosea often uses the image of a broken marriage to show God's pain.

For today: When something takes the place of God in the heart, it gradually becomes harder to return. Today you can ask yourself what distracts you from him, and take a small step back toward him with a sincere prayer.
exp.10:10:
It says that the people of Israel will return from Egypt and Assyria quickly, like birds that fly and like doves that come back to their nest. "They shall tremble" means they will come trembling or agitated, and "I will place them" is the meaning of the words for "I will place them." God promises to return them to their homes.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel (called Ephraim) had turned away from God and faced judgment, with exile and foreign rule. Even so, in this chapter God says he will not destroy his people completely, because he is God and not a man. Scholars debate whether the promise refers only to the return from exile or also to something broader and future.

Today it reminds us that God disciplines, but does not abandon. If you have wandered away, you can return to him with confidence, because his desire is to restore you and give you a home.
exp.2:2:
Hosea tells the woman he bought: "You will stay with me many days. You will not be unfaithful, and you will not belong to another man, and I too will not be with you as a husband." The word "unfaithful" here means to be a prostitute or to live in infidelity.

The phrase "for me" in this verse means "belonging to me."

Hosea speaks by command of God. His marriage to an unfaithful woman is a picture of God's love for Israel, which had gone after other gods. The following verse applies this: Israel would spend many days without king or worship, in a time of waiting and correction, before returning to seek God.

For today: God's love does not give up, but it also knows how to set limits in order to heal. If something has taken the place of God in your heart, He invites you to a time of stillness, to letting it go, and to returning to Him with trust.
exp.12:3:
God reminds the Israelites who he is: the Lord who brought them out of Egypt, and their only God. He tells them they must not acknowledge any other god, because there is no saviour besides him. The verse's "yet" in the opening words means "but," and "beside me" means "besides me" or "apart from me."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had made idols of silver, including calves they kissed in worship. God brings to their memory their history: he freed them from Egypt and cared for them in the wilderness. Their error was forgetting the one who had saved them and trusting in things made by human hands.

For today: ask yourself what you are trusting in to feel secure, such as money, work, or the approval of others. Those things cannot save you. Remember how God has sustained you in other times, and place your trust in him again.
exp.12:9:
God asks Israel where the king is in whom it trusted. He asks them to look and see whether that king, with his judges and princes, can deliver the people and their cities. The question is ironic: there is no one who can save them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations, and they leaned on human leaders more than on God. Now judgment is coming, but the verse before says that their help is in God. Scholars debate exactly which king or moment is in view, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: examine where you place your ultimate trust, whether in a leader, a government, money, or your own plan. Those things may help, but they cannot save you. Turn your confidence back to God, who still offers help.
exp.12:0:
It says that the tribe of Ephraim, the largest in the northern kingdom, had great authority: when it spoke, people felt respect. He was "exalted," that is, honored and lifted up. But he sinned by worshiping Baal, a false god, and with that he "died," for he was left spiritually ruined and under judgment.

Here the prophet Hosea speaks on behalf of God, before the fall of the kingdom of Israel. Ephraim represents the whole northern kingdom. God reminds it of its former influence to show that the idol led it to ruin. The verses that follow show that the sin kept growing worse.

For today: a position, success, or the respect of others does not protect us if we place our hearts in something that is not God. It is worth examining what holds first place in our lives and humbly returning to Him.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that the people offered sacrifices to God and ate the meat, but God did not accept them. The words "visit their sin" mean that he will hold them accountable for their wrongs. "They shall return to Egypt" means they will go back to a situation like slavery; some understand this literally and others as a picture of punishment and exile.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. They built many altars and performed many rituals, but they ignored God's law and had forgotten him. Their religion was outward show, without obedience or sincere love.

For today: it is not enough to keep rituals, go to church, or give offerings if the heart is far from God. Ask him to teach you to obey him truly, with humility and sincerity, not merely out of habit.
exp.9:5:
It says that the golden calf that Israel worshiped at Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria as a gift for King Jareb. "Gift" means a present or tribute. The phrase about Israel being ashamed of its own counsel means that Israel will be put to shame by its own plans. Ephraim, who represents the northern kingdom, will suffer shame.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, which trusted in idols and in alliances with other nations instead of trusting in Him. "Jareb" is not a clear name: it may be a title of the king of Assyria, meaning something like "the contending king," or a reference to a particular king. Scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: whatever we put in place of God, whether money, power, or our own plans, ends up failing and leaving us ashamed. Let us ask God to guide our decisions and trust Him first.
exp.11:6:
