The verse in your reader's text is Hosea 12:7, which reads: "He is a merchant, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress."

The verse calls on the reader to return to their God. The word for this means to turn back, to change direction. It also calls for practicing mercy, which means steadfast love and kindness, and judgment, which here means justice. And it calls the reader to wait on God continually, that is, to trust in Him patiently and without growing weary.

The prophet Hosea speaks to the people of the northern kingdom, called Ephraim or Israel. He reminds them of their ancestor Jacob, who wrestled, wept, and sought God at Bethel. Then he rebukes them, because they used false scales, oppressed others, and considered themselves innocent because they were rich. God offers them the chance to return.

Today, true faith shows in daily dealings. Examine your work and your business: be honest, just, and compassionate, and trust in God more than in your money.
exp.3:8:
It says that the people and the priest will end up the same: both are guilty. God says he will punish their ways, that is, he will hold them accountable for how they live. The phrase about repaying them according to their deeds means that they will receive the consequences of what they did.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom of Israel. The priests were meant to teach God's law, but according to the chapter, they took advantage of the people's sin and did not guide them well. That is why the people and their leaders fall under the same judgment. Scholars agree that the sin belonged to the leaders as well as to the people.

For today: those who lead others, in the church or at home, carry a greater responsibility. And those who follow a leader cannot make excuses. Each person must seek God and live honestly before Him.
exp.8:12:
Hosea says that he saw Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, likened to the city of Tyre: established in a beautiful and secure place. But that well-being will not last, because Ephraim will have to hand over its children to the enemy who kills. Some words in the Hebrew are difficult, and the translations vary a little.

The prophet Hosea speaks, bringing God's message. Israel was prosperous, but it had filled itself with idolatry and disloyalty. For this reason God announces judgment: the peace they saw would not protect them from the consequences of turning away from Him.

For today: comfort and success are not proof that everything is right with God. Ask yourself honestly in what you trust most: in what you have, or in the Lord. Return to Him while there is still time.
exp.13:0:
It says that Israel must return to God, because its sin made it fall. "Return" means turning back, changing course and coming back to Him. The word "unto" in the King James is an old way of saying "to," so the sentence on that word has to be rewritten for a word of the verse: "Return" and "fallen" are the key words here, and the verse's own phrasing carries the meaning. God not only points out the fall, He also invites them to rise.

The prophet Hosea speaks, in God's name, to the people of Israel, the northern kingdom. This is the last chapter of the book, after many warnings about idolatry and lack of faithfulness. The verses that follow offer words for prayer: asking for forgiveness, not trusting in Assyria or in war horses, and giving up idols. It ends with the hope that God has mercy.

For today: if there is something in your life that drew you away from God, do not wait until you feel perfect. Go to Him today with a sincere prayer, acknowledge your mistake, and trust in His mercy.
exp.1:13:
God says that, in spite of everything, he himself will draw his people back with tenderness. Here "allure" means to persuade, to draw someone gently and with affection. He will lead her into the wilderness, a place without distractions, and there he will speak to her tenderly, that is, with words of love and comfort.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel, compared to an unfaithful wife, went after the Baals, false gods, and credited its blessings to them. God announces judgment, but it does not end there: this verse is the turning point toward restoration. The wilderness recalls the time after Egypt, when the people came to know God up close.

For today: when you feel far from God or guilty, do not run from him. Set aside a while for silence, without noise or screens, and listen. He calls you not to condemn you, but to speak to you with love and restore you.
exp.1:1:
God invites the children to "plead" with their mother, that is, to call her to account and confront her. She is Israel, seen as an unfaithful wife. God says that he no longer recognizes her as his wife. He asks her to put away her idolatry and disloyalty, and her adultery, which showed on her face and on her breast, that is, in plain sight of everyone.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, at a time when Israel was worshiping other gods. The children's names, Ammi, meaning "my people," and Ruhama, meaning "shown mercy," mean the call still carries hope. Many understand that the warning aims to lead the people to repentance, not only to punish them.

For today: if there is something in your life that has taken the place of God, do not hide it. Acknowledge it honestly, return to him, and seek help from mature brothers and sisters who will speak to you with truth and kindness.
exp.13:2:
This verse says that the people, returning to God, acknowledge that they cannot trust in Assyria (Asshur) to save them, nor in horses, which represent military strength. It also promises to stop calling the idols made by their own hands their gods. The final reason is that in God the fatherless, the one who has no one, finds compassion. "Asshur" is the name of Assyria, the nation Israel had turned to for help.

The prophet Hosea speaks to Israel, which had sought help in alliances with other nations and in idols. God invites them to repent, and even suggests the words they can say to him. Then, in the following verse, God responds by promising to heal their rebellion and to love them freely.

For today: examine what you place your security in, such as money, influence, or your own plans. Hand them over to God sincerely, and come to him as you are, with your emptiness and needs, trusting that he will receive you with mercy.
exp.9:3:
They talked a great deal, but their promises were false. They made agreements and swore oaths without any intention of keeping them. So God's judgment would spring up like wormwood, a bitter and poisonous plant that grows in the furrows where good fruit should have been. The phrase "swearing falsely" means making promises with deceit or without sincerity.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). The people had a divided heart: they worshiped idols and trusted in kings and human alliances, not in the LORD. Their broken agreements with others and with God brought injustice and judgment as a result.

For today: take care with your words and your promises. If you say you will do something, keep it with honesty, above all before God. A life of empty words produces bitter fruit, but sincerity and faithfulness build trust and honor the Lord.
exp.1:17:
God promises to make a covenant with the animals of the field, the birds, and the creeping creatures, so that they will no longer be a threat. He also says he will break the bow, the sword, and war, that is, he will remove weapons and conflict from the land. As a result, his people will be able to rest peacefully and without fear. The phrase "they will lie down safely" means "they will rest in confidence."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, who had been unfaithful to him by worshiping the Baals. Even so, God promises to restore the relationship, like a husband who forgives. Many understand this peace as an image of complete reconciliation; whether it refers to a future or a spiritual fulfillment, interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: when fear or insecurity keeps you from resting, remember that God is the one who gives true peace. Speak to him honestly, entrust your fears to him, and seek to live close to him, who promises to restore what is broken.
exp.4:8:
Ephraim, which represents the northern kingdom of Israel, will be destroyed and left desolate when the day comes that God brings judgment upon it. The word "desolate" here means laid waste, left in ruins. God adds that He is not acting by surprise: among the tribes of Israel He had already made known something certain, a true and firm warning.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people had been unfaithful to Him, worshiping idols and forgetting their covenant with Him. That is why the punishment was not arbitrary: they already knew what God expected and what would happen if they abandoned Him.

For today: God speaks to us clearly in His Word because He loves us. When we feel His correction, we can see it as an invitation to return to Him before the consequences grow.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel) and Judah both came to see that they were sick and wounded because of their sin. But instead of seeking God, Ephraim went to Assyria and asked the king named Jareb for help. The name Jareb may be a personal name or a title, and its meaning is uncertain. That king could not heal them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He is judging his people because they turned away from him and looked for security in alliances with foreign powers. God warns them that no human help could cure what only he can heal. But the passage ends with hope: God hopes they will acknowledge their sin and seek him.

For today: when you feel wounded, guilty, or afraid, do not run first to solutions that cannot heal the heart. Go to God first, with sincerity. He corrects, but he also restores.
exp.9:7:
The high places of Aven, where Israel sinned, will be destroyed. Aven means "wickedness" or "emptiness," and it seems to be a scornful name for Bethel, the place where they set up a golden calf. Where there were once altars, thorns and thistles will grow. In their great fear, the people will say to the mountains, "Cover us," and to the hills, "Fall on us." That is, they would rather die than face judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had mixed the worship of God with idols and trusted in their king and their alliances. Hosea announces that Assyria would carry them into captivity and that their false refuges would not save them.

For today: examine the things you rely on more than God, such as money, success, or empty religiosity. Surrender them to Him today, before they collapse, and seek refuge in Him, who forgives the one who repents.
exp.10:0:
God loved Israel from its beginnings, when it was like a child, and he brought it out of Egypt, calling it "my son." The word translated as "child" speaks of the people's youth, that is, of its beginning as a nation.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He reminds the Israelites of the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim, how much he cared for them during the exodus. Even so, they turned away and served the Baals, false gods. The verses that follow show God as a father who teaches his son to walk. In Matthew 2:15, the New Testament quotes this phrase when speaking of Jesus; many see it as a connection between Israel and Christ.

God loved us first, before we responded to him. Today you can remember how he has cared for you, even when you sometimes did not notice it, and return to him with gratitude and trust.
exp.1:8:
God says that he is going to come back and take away what he had given: the grain and the wine when the time of harvest arrives, and also the wool and the flax with which she covered her nakedness. "Return" means come back; the "right time" is the proper moment, the ripeness; "nakedness" is the shame of her poverty.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, described as an unfaithful wife. She credited her blessings to Baal and to her lovers, without recognizing that they came from God. That is why he takes away his gifts, not as simple punishment, but so that she will wake up and return to him, her first husband.

For today: let us remember that everything good we have comes from God. Let us give thanks today instead of trusting in money, success, or things that cannot sustain us, and return to him with sincerity.
exp.3:15:
This verse says Israel has behaved like a stubborn young heifer that will not be led or accept the yoke. Then God asks a question with a tone of reproach: how can he now care for them as lambs in an open, quiet field? To shepherd means to tend a flock, and a wide, safe pasture is what is meant. The idea is that someone who rejects the shepherd cannot expect the peace of the meadow.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people practiced idolatry and mixed their worship with pagan practices. God warns Judah not to follow that path and calls them not to go to Gilgal or Beth-aven, places of corrupted worship. Some understand the question as a warning of judgment; others, as a lament.

For today: we cannot ask for the protection of the Shepherd while we resist his guidance. Today you can hand over a specific area where you have been stubborn and ask him to teach you to obey.
exp.3:3:
It says that no one should argue with or accuse another, because the problem is not in this one or that one, but in the whole people. "Strive" means to fight or dispute, and "reprove" means to correct or accuse. The people are compared to those who oppose the priest, that is, they reject the one who was supposed to teach them the law of God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just accused Israel of lying, stealing, murdering and committing adultery. Here he seems to say that blaming one another no longer helps, since everyone is responsible. Some scholars also understand that the priest is being accused, as is seen later; the verse is difficult and is translated in several ways.

For today: before pointing out the faults of others, examine your own heart. Acknowledge your part, seek the Word of God with humility, and let it correct you first.
exp.8:5:
It says that the people of Israel go into exile because of the destruction that is coming. Egypt will gather them, that is, it will be their refuge or their place of captivity, and Memphis, an Egyptian city famous for its tombs, will bury them. What they valued most, the treasures they had silver for, will be overrun by thorns, and nettles will grow in their abandoned houses.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel (also called Ephraim). He warns that their idolatry and injustice will bring judgment. Their feasts and sacrifices do not please God because their hearts are far from Him. Many understand that Egypt here is a symbol of returning to slavery, though some take it literally.

For today: let us not confuse religion with a sincere relationship with God. Let us examine whether what we care for most, such as money and possessions, occupies the place that only God deserves. Let us return to Him with our whole heart, before what we love is left empty.
exp.5:9:
God says he has seen something horrible among his people. The word "horrible" here means something frightening, a shameful condition. The phrase about spiritual unfaithfulness refers to Ephraim, who represents the northern kingdom, leaving God to follow other gods. The idea of being stained means that all of Israel was marked by that betrayal.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Just before this, he has mentioned crimes of violence, including by priests who were supposed to guide the people. God does not speak with indifference but like a husband wounded by unfaithfulness, an image Hosea uses throughout the book. His complaint is serious, but the book also shows his desire to restore his people.

For today: God sees what we sometimes hide. We can ask ourselves what things we have placed our trust or our heart in above him. With sincerity, let us return to him, who forgives and restores.
exp.12:4:
God tells his people that he "knew" them while they were in the wilderness, in a dry land with no resources. Here "knew" means to care for, accompany, and love closely, not merely to know who they were. It was God who sustained them when there was no water and no food.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel (also called Ephraim). He reminds them of the time after leaving Egypt, when they depended completely on him. He does this because, once they were prosperous, they became filled with pride and forgot God, as the following verse says. For this reason the people are warned of judgment.

For today: Remember the dry seasons when God sustained you. Remembering it helps you stay thankful and humble when things go well, and not forget where your help comes from.
exp.4:11:
He says that God himself will be like a moth to Ephraim and like rottenness to Judah. A moth eats away at clothing, and rottenness decays wood, and both destroy slowly, without making any noise. Ephraim refers to the northern kingdom, Israel, and Judah to the southern kingdom.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The leaders of Judah had moved the boundary stones, that is, they were violating what had been set in place, and Ephraim was following human commands and not the voice of God. For this reason God announces a judgment that wears away from within. Later, they will seek help from Assyria, but it will not be able to heal them.

For today: do not make light of small sins that are repeated, for they wear away life in silence. Return soon to God, who is the one who truly heals, and do not seek salvation in other sources.
exp.9:9:
God says that he will punish Israel whenever he wishes. Enemy peoples will gather against them, and they will be bound, like animals tied to the plow. The phrase "in their two furrows" is hard to translate; some understand it as "their two sins" or "their double guilt," and others prefer to read "their two eyes" or another reading. There are several interpretations.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. The people had false altars and had turned away from God for a long time, and God announces that their sin would bring judgment.

For today: God corrects because he loves, and he calls us not to harden our hearts. If you notice something in your life that is pulling you away from God, do not wait for the consequence to arrive; seek the Lord now, with humility, and let him teach you the right path.
exp.3:17:
Israel had gone to ruin: its drink had become sour (some understand this to refer to the feasting and drunkenness, since the Hebrew text is difficult), and it gave itself over to unfaithfulness persistently, that is, with stubbornness. Its rulers loved gifts, that is, bribes and presents, and this filled them with shame.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, also called Ephraim. The people worshiped idols and turned away from God like a stubborn heifer. The leaders, instead of caring for justice, sought their own gain.

Today this invites us to examine what we truly love. If money or comfort leads us to keep silent about the truth or to be unjust, we drift away from God. Ask Him for a faithful and honest heart, and act with integrity even when no one sees you.
exp.9:13:
God says he is about to deliver a hard blow against Israel: there will be a roar of war among its towns, and its strongholds will be destroyed. He compares this to what Shalman did at Beth-arbel, a destruction so cruel that the mother was dashed to the ground together with her children. The word "tumult" in the verse means the din of war, and "strongholds" are the walled cities.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had trusted in its army and in its own way, and not in the Lord. It had sown wickedness and would now reap deception. Who Shalman was and where Beth-arbel stood is uncertain; scholars have interpreted this in several ways.

For today: do not put your security in your strength, your money, or your plans. Seek the Lord with humility, sow justice and mercy, and trust in him.
exp.8:11:
God says that even if the children of Ephraim (the kingdom of Israel) grow up, he will take them away from among men, meaning they will vanish or die. He then adds with grief: "woe to them" when he departs from them.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier he recalls how he delighted to find Israel, like grapes in the wilderness, but they gave themselves over to idolatry at Baal-peor. Because of this judgment comes: their families and their future will be affected. Some scholars see here a warning of war and exile, though the text itself gives no further detail.

For today: the worst punishment is living far from God. Do not take your relationship with him lightly. Return to God with sincerity, and pray for your family so that it grows under his care.
exp.0:9:
Says that, despite the punishment announced, the people of Israel will become too many to count, like the sand of the sea. And in the very place where God told them "You are not my people," one day He will say to them, "You are the sons of the living God." "Yet" means "even so."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier, the names of his children, Lo-ruhama ("not pitied") and Lo-ammi ("not my people"), announced judgment for Israel's unfaithfulness. Here the message changes: judgment is not the final word. This recalls the promise made to Abraham about his descendants. The New Testament quotes this passage in Romans 9:25-26, applying it also to people from all nations.

For today: if you feel that your failures have left you far from God, remember that His mercy can change your story. Return to Him with confidence, and let Him call you His son or daughter.
exp.11:10:
God says that he himself spoke to the prophets, that he gave them many visions and messages, and that through them he used parables or examples so that the people would understand. "I multiplied prophecy" means that he sent word after word, again and again.

Here God speaks to the people of Israel, who are called Ephraim, and who boasted of their wealth and believed themselves free of blame. God reminds them that he has been their God since Egypt and that they have not lacked warning. The verses that follow show that, even so, the people kept on in idolatry (Gilgal, altars).

For today: God continues to speak with clarity, and it is not his fault if we do not listen. Before trusting in what we have achieved, it is wise to open the Bible with humility and let God correct us.
exp.13:5:
It says that the restored people will grow like a healthy tree. Its branches will spread out. Its beauty will be like that of the olive tree, an evergreen and valuable tree, and its fragrance will be pleasant like the cedars and forests of Lebanon, famous for their scent.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from God through idols and rebellion, but now God promises to heal them and love them wholeheartedly, because his anger has passed. This is a promise of restoration for whoever returns to him.

For today: if you feel far from God or damaged by your mistakes, you can return to him with confidence. He forgives and also makes a new life grow. That growth is usually gradual, like that of a tree, so stay close to God each day.
exp.1:4:
Here it is said that the mother of these children was unfaithful and acted without shame. Here "played the harlot" means to be unfaithful, to prostitute oneself, and "lovers" are the men she goes after in place of her husband. She believes they give her everything she needs: food, water, clothing (wool and flax), oil and drink.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who seeks other gods, such as Baal, and credits to them the blessings that really come from the Lord. That is why God announces a punishment, in the hope that she will recognize her error and return to Him, as the following verses say.

Today we can ask ourselves to whom we give thanks for what we have. It is easy to trust in work, money or success and forget that every good thing comes from God. Let us offer a sincere prayer of gratitude and place our trust in Him again.
exp.1:5:
God says that he is going to block the way of Israel, compared to an unfaithful wife. He will place thorns and a wall of brambles, so that she gets lost and cannot find her way.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people were following Baal, a Canaanite god, thinking that he gave them bread, wool, and oil. For this reason God blocks those paths. His purpose, according to the verses that follow, is that she will recognize who was truly sustaining her and will want to return to him.

For today: sometimes God allows obstacles to stop us when we go after things that take us away from him. If something blocks your way, do not harden your heart; ask yourself humbly what you are seeking and whether God is calling you to return to him.
exp.1:20:
He says that when the time of restoration comes, God himself will answer, and his answer will set all of creation in motion. God answers the heavens, the heavens answer the earth, and the earth answers the grain, the wine, and the oil. Here "answer" works like an echo: one thing responds to another.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful to him, and God announces that he will again bind himself to his people with justice, mercy, and faithfulness. This promise shows that when the relationship with God is restored, order and provision are restored with it. Many understand it to point to a future blessing, and the details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: when you feel far from God or in need, draw near to him with confidence. He listens and responds, and his goodness often comes through simple, everyday things.
exp.5:0:
It is an invitation to return to God. The verse's "Come" means "come," and the call to "return" points to turning back, a word the verse itself gives as "return unto the Lord." The word "torn" here means that God tore or took away, like a wound. God corrected, but he can also heal and bind up. So the same God who struck is the one who cures.

The speaker is the people of Israel, or someone urging them to repent, in a time of judgment and suffering. But in verse 4 God tells them that their love is passing, like the morning mist. For this reason some think this repentance was superficial, and others see it as a good example of turning back to God.

Today, when you go through pain or failure, do not run from God. Return to him with sincerity, trusting that he can heal what is broken.
exp.10:1:
This verse says that, while God was calling Israel, the people kept moving away from Him. Instead of answering Him, they sacrificed to the Baals, which were false gods of Canaan, and burned incense to carved images, that is, to the sculpted idols.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century BC, to the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). First He recalls His love as a father: He brought Israel out of Egypt and cared for it like a small child. That is why the pain is greater: the people forgot who had cared for them and went after other gods.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place that belongs to God: money, success, comfort. When He calls us, we sometimes pretend not to hear. Remembering how much He has cared for us helps us return and answer Him with trust and gratitude.
exp.10:5:
This verse says the war will reach the cities of Israel and destroy their towns and villages. It means that the coming conflict will bring total destruction to their settlements. The sword will fall on their cities, and their branches will be consumed. Some scholars also understand that it may allude to their false leaders or to their political alliances.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. God had shown them love like a careful father, but they did not want to return to him. For this reason judgment would come, and Assyria would be the power that would dominate them. Even so, the verses that follow show God's pain at having to correct them.

For today: when we trust only in our own plans and reject God's guidance, we suffer the consequences. Today you can ask him for wisdom before you decide, remembering that his correction comes from a love that does not give up.
exp.7:2:
Israel is said to have rejected and left behind what is good, that is, God and his ways. That is why an enemy will pursue them.

The word "cast off" means that they abandoned or left alone what they had been given; "the thing that is good" can be understood as God himself, his law, and what is right.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom. The people had broken the covenant, made idols, and set up kings without consulting God. Earlier, the text already announces that a judgment will come swiftly, like an eagle. God warns that abandoning him has consequences. Many scholars see Assyria as the enemy, although the text does not name it here.

Today we can ask ourselves which good things we have let slip: prayer, honesty, the Word. Saying "we know you" is not enough if we do not live according to it. Let us return to God today with simplicity and obedience.
exp.5:4:
God says that, because of the people's hardness, he sent his prophets to cut them down, that is, to strike them down and confront them, and that his words were like a sentence that kills. "Kill" here is strong language: God's word announces judgment. And those judgments will come into the open, clearly and plainly, like the sun rising.

God speaks through Hosea. He has just said that the faithfulness of Ephraim and Judah, that is, their loyal love, is passing, like the morning cloud or the dew. Their repentance was shallow. Some understand that "hewed" refers to the harsh preaching of the prophets; the phrase is not entirely literal.

For today: it is not enough to feel sorry for a moment. Ask God for a steady heart, one that listens to his correction and turns it into daily obedience, not just passing emotion.
exp.8:3:
In exile, Israel will no longer be able to offer wine to God or sacrifices that please Him. Their bread will be like "bread of mourners", that is, the bread of people who are grieving a death, which according to the law made anyone who ate it unclean. That bread would only serve to satisfy hunger, not to be taken to the house of the Lord.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel (called Ephraim) in the eighth century B.C. There was idolatry and unfaithfulness, and God warns that they will lose the land and live among foreign peoples. The exact details of that exile are understood in several ways, but the central message is clear.

For today: worship is not a simple ritual. If my heart is far from God, my offerings and my songs lose their meaning. Today I can draw near to Him sincerely, acknowledging my failures and returning to Him with humility.
exp.0:3:
God tells Hosea to name his first child Jezreel. God announces that he will soon judge the house of Jehu and bring an end to the northern kingdom, called Israel.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea, at a time when the people had turned away from God. Jezreel was the site of a massacre in the days of Jehu (2 Kings 9–10). Scholars explain in various ways why God judges it there: some think Jehu was too violent, and others that his family continued in idolatry. The child's name functions as a prophetic sign.

For today: God sees what we have done, even what seemed justified. Let us ask him to examine our hearts and guide us to obey him with humility.
exp.4:10:
Ephraim, who is the northern kingdom of Israel, is oppressed and broken under God's judgment. "Oppressed" means mistreated or crushed. "Walked after" means to go after something, to follow it. The reason is that Ephraim chose to follow "commandments" that did not come from God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He had given his truth to the people, but they preferred other orders. Some think this refers to decrees from their kings, others to rules tied to idolatry. The Hebrew text is difficult and not certain. That is why God announces punishment and, later on, shows that seeking help from Assyria would not heal them.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we are following. Before obeying trends, pressures, or traditions, it is wise to compare them with the Word of God and ask him for wisdom to choose his way.
exp.13:7:
Ephraim, that is, the people of Israel, recognizes that the idols are of no use: "What have I to do any more with idols?" Then God answers that he will listen to his people and care for them. He is compared to a green fir tree, a leafy tree that gives shade. Under his shade there is protection, and from God comes all fruit.

The one who speaks at the end is God, responding to Ephraim's repentance. Hosea closes his book with a promise of restoration after speaking of judgment and unfaithfulness. The verses before it show a people blossoming again. It is an invitation to return to God and to leave behind what once filled the heart.

For today: identify what has taken God's place in your life, such as money, fame, or fear. Say to him sincerely: "What have I to do any more with this?" Return to him, and trust that from his care true fruit will grow in you.
exp.7:0:
It says that someone must put a trumpet to the mouth, that is, give a loud warning. An enemy will come swiftly like an eagle against the house of the Lord, because the people have broken the covenant, that is, they violated it, and rebelled against his law. The name of God appears here as the Lord.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, the northern kingdom. The trumpet was an alarm signal before an attack. God warns of a coming judgment. Many understand that the "eagle" refers to an invader, probably Assyria, although the text does not name it here. "The house of the Lord" may refer to his people or to his land.

For today: it is not enough to say that we know God, as the text goes on to say, if we do not live in obedience. Today we can honestly examine where we have failed him, return to him, and obey him from the heart.
exp.8:0:
God tells Israel not to rejoice or be glad as the other nations do. The reason is that the people had been unfaithful to God. Here, the word "whoring" means spiritual unfaithfulness, that is, worshiping other gods. The "reward" refers to the payment the people believed they were receiving from those idols. The "cornfloors" were the places where grain was threshed after the harvest.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim). Many understand that the people credited their harvests to fertility gods, such as Baal, and not to the Lord. That is why it is announced that the harvest will fail and that there will be exile.

For today: check to whom you give credit for your blessings. Thank God, and do not place your trust in money or in success.
exp.2:1:
Hosea obeys God and buys this woman. He pays fifteen "dineros," that is, pieces or shekels of silver, and also a homer and a half of barley. A homer was a large measure of grain. Some think the total was a price similar to that of a slave, but this is not certain.

God speaks to the prophet Hosea. He tells him to love an adulterous woman, and the text suggests she is his wife Gomer. Her story is a picture of God's love for Israel, which had turned away to other gods, yet whom God did not abandon.

For today: God seeks us out and rescues us even when we have failed him. Receiving that love invites us to return to him with humility. It also encourages us to treat with patience and grace those who have failed us, without ignoring the truth.
exp.3:7:
It says that the priests "eat up" the sin of the people, that is, they feed on it. The sin offerings were given to the priests (Leviticus 6:26). Here it seems that the priests benefit if the people keep on sinning so that they receive more. The phrase "they set their heart on their iniquity" means that they desire and long for that wickedness.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom, Israel. He accuses the priests of forgetting the law and not teaching the people. Therefore the people were perishing for lack of knowledge. Some interpreters see here a criticism of greed; the text gives no further detail.

For today: those who teach or lead others should seek the good of people, not their own gain. And all of us can ask ourselves: am I more interested in the truth of God or in what I gain from it? Let us ask God for a humble and faithful heart.
exp.1:12:
It says God will call Israel to account for the days when she offered incense to the Baals, false gods of Canaan. Burning incense is what she did. The earrings and the jewels are what she wore as she dressed herself up for the festival, and she went after her lovers, that is, the idols, and forgot me. The saddest thing is that forgetting.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who credits her harvests to others and not to her husband. That is why judgment is coming. But the following verse shows the end of the punishment: God will lead her into the wilderness, speak to her heart, and give her hope.

For today: examine which things have taken the place of God in your heart, such as money, success, or the approval of others. Thank Him for what you have, and return to Him, who corrects in order to restore.
exp.2:0:
This verse tells how God speaks to Hosea again and commands him to love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress. God compares this love with his own love toward Israel, a people who turn to other gods. "Flagons of wine" probably refers to cakes of raisins, used at feasts of pagan worship, though some understand it simply as a love of pleasure.

The Lord is speaking, and Hosea is the prophet. God uses Hosea's married life as a living sign: just as Hosea loves an unfaithful woman, God continues to love his unfaithful people. It is not known with certainty whether this woman is Gomer, the one from Hosea 1, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: God's love does not depend on our faithfulness. Today you can return to Him with confidence, and also strive to love with patience those who have failed you.
exp.3:2:
Therefore, it says, because of the people's sins, the land will go into mourning. Everyone who lives in it will grow weak and waste away, along with the beasts of the field, the birds of the sky, and even the fish of the sea.

The word "mourn" here means that the land will be sad, as at a funeral. The word "languish" means that they will grow weak. The word "die" means that they will perish.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. God brings an accusation against his people because there was no longer any truth, mercy, or knowledge of him, and lying, stealing, adultery, and violence were everywhere. Many understand that creation suffers because of human wickedness. Some think the text refers to drought or to ruin from an invasion; the text does not spell this out.

Today, this verse reminds us that our choices affect other people and the world around us. We can seek God, live with honesty, and show mercy, caring for creation as well.
exp.8:4:
This verse is a question that God asks through the prophet. It asks what the Israelites will do when their sacred festivals come, the solemn day and the feast of the Lord. The question suggests that they will not be able to celebrate them as they did before.

Hosea speaks to Ephraim, the name given to the northern kingdom, Israel. Because of their unfaithfulness and their idolatry, the prophet announces that they will be carried into exile, to Assyria and Egypt. There they will not have the temple and will not be able to offer sacrifices, and their food would be unclean according to the law.

For today: let us not take worship and spiritual privileges for granted. If our hearts turn away from God, religious practices become empty. Let us seek a sincere relationship with Him, not merely carry out rituals.
exp.11:13:
God says that he brought Israel out of Egypt through a prophet, Moses, and through a prophet he cared for them. But Ephraim, who stands for the northern kingdom, angered him bitterly, that is, with sins that deeply offend him. Because of this, the guilt for their killings and violence will fall upon him, and his Lord will return his shame to him, that is, the contempt and mockery he showed toward God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, who calls Israel to repentance. Earlier he recalled how Jacob was humble and worked as a shepherd. Now he sets that past against the idolatry and injustice of the people. God reminds them that he always guided them with care, but they repaid him badly.

For today: God has cared for us more than we notice. Before we harden our hearts, let us remember his goodness and respond with gratitude and obedience, not with pride.
exp.6:2:
This verse says that the people of Israel, with their evil deeds and their lies, amuse and please their king and their rulers. Instead of being ashamed of sin, they celebrate it. The rulers are the leaders or authorities of the kingdom.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim, with its capital Samaria). God wanted to heal his people, but every time he drew near, more deceit and corruption appeared. The verses that follow show a court full of betrayal and drunkenness. Some scholars think it refers to political intrigues of that time, although the text does not give all the details.

For today: let us examine whom we try to please. It is easy to applaud lies or injustice in order to be liked or to gain advantages. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth with love, even when it costs us.
exp.0:7:
This verse tells us that Gomer, the wife of the prophet Hosea, stopped nursing their daughter Lo-ruhamah and became pregnant again. A son was born. "Weaned" means that the child no longer drank breast milk, which suggests that a few years had passed. To give birth is to bring a child into the world.

God spoke to Hosea, and the life of his family became a message for Israel. The name Lo-ruhamah means "not pitied," and it showed that the northern kingdom had fallen into idolatry and would soon face judgment. The next child will be given the name Lo-ammi, "not my people." But the passage ends with hope: God promises to restore his people.

For today: even when our mistakes have consequences, God does not stop speaking to us with hope. We can return to him sincerely, trusting that his mercy is greater than our past.
exp.5:3:
God asks with sorrow: "What shall I do with you, Ephraim? What shall I do with you, Judah?" He tells them that their goodness, that is, their love and loyalty toward Him, lasts only as long as a morning cloud or the early dew, which the sun soon makes disappear. Ephraim was the common name for the northern kingdom, Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Just before this, the people had said beautiful words about returning to God and knowing Him. But God sees that their commitment is passing and shallow. That is why, in the verses that follow, He makes clear that what He desires most is mercy and the knowledge of Him, not only religious offerings.

For today: religious feelings that fade quickly are not enough. Ask God for a steady love and show it through small daily acts: praying, forgiving, helping, and obeying, even when you do not feel enthusiastic.
exp.6:8:
Verse 9 says that foreign peoples have been devouring the strength and wealth of Ephraim (the northern kingdom, Israel), and he has not even noticed. Gray hairs have also appeared on him, a sign that he was growing weaker and aging, and he did not notice that either. "Strength" here means force or resources, and "gray hairs" points to the gray hairs themselves, that is, to the wear and decline.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was seeking alliances with other nations instead of calling on God, and those alliances were wearing it down. Some think this refers to tribute paid to Assyria; the text does not spell this out. The central point is spiritual blindness: he was declining and did not recognize it.

For today: sometimes sin, carelessness, or bad habits wear us down little by little without our noticing. Let us ask God to show us honestly where we stand, and return to Him soon, before the damage grows.
exp.3:1:
This verse describes the sins of the people. "Swearing falsely" means taking an oath that is untrue; "stealing" means taking what belongs to someone else; "committing adultery" means being unfaithful in marriage. The verse says these evils "broke out," meaning they became common and widespread. "Blood touched blood" probably refers to one murder after another, without a pause, though some understand it as violence that stains everything.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to Israel, the northern kingdom. He brings a charge against them, as in a courtroom, because they had abandoned truth, mercy, and the knowledge of God. The verses that follow show that this sin also harmed the land and its creatures.

For today: when we truly know God, it shows in everyday life. Today you can choose one concrete action, such as keeping your word or being honest even when it costs you, in order to live with truth and mercy.
exp.5:2:
This verse says the people want to know God and to keep knowing him every day. It compares God to the dawn, which comes up with certainty, and to the rain that waters the earth. "Prepared" is the sense here, and the early and latter rains are the spring and autumn rains, needed for the harvests.

Here the people of Israel speak, urging one another to return to God after the punishment. But in the verses that follow, God answers that their love is like a morning cloud and dew that soon passes away. In other words, the words sound good, but the heart was not yet steady.

For today: knowing God is not a passing emotion but a daily path. Set aside a regular time to read his Word and pray, and let that faith show in your conduct, not only in your words.
exp.6:0:
When God wanted to heal Israel, the wickedness of Ephraim came to light, and the evil of Samaria as well. "Ephraim" names the northern kingdom, and Samaria was its capital. "They practice deceit" means that they acted with lies and fraud. The text adds two images: a thief who breaks into houses, and a robber who plunders from outside.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century B.C., to a northern kingdom full of corruption, injustice and idolatry. When God tried to restore them, the people showed their true heart. Interpreters see the image of the thief and the robber as both internal disorder and external threat, and they do not always agree.

For today: when God confronts us, it is not to humiliate us but to heal us. If something hidden comes to light in your life, do not hide it or make excuses; bring it to God honestly and let Him heal it.
exp.3:13:
It says that God will not punish the daughters for their prostitution or the daughters-in-law for their adultery, because the men themselves do worse things: they offer sacrifices together with prostitutes. "Visit" means to call to account or to punish. "Whores" are prostitutes. "Bad women" probably refers to prostitutes tied to the pagan cults. It concludes that a people without understanding will fall.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, which had given itself over to idolatry in the fertility cults. God shows them that the fathers and husbands are the main guilty parties, since they were setting the bad example. Some scholars think God here denounces the hypocrisy of men who blamed the women; others see it as a judgment in which God lets corruption run its course. Both readings are possible.

For today: those of us who lead others, as parents, leaders, or teachers, cannot demand what we do not live ourselves. Let us ask God for understanding and begin by examining our own hearts.
exp.12:13:
God promises to rescue his people from the power of the grave and from death. The grave is the place of the dead. He says that he himself will be the destruction of death, that is, he will put it to an end. The final phrase, "repentance shall be hid from mine eyes," means that God will not change his mind about this promise.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Before and after this verse, he announces judgment on Ephraim (Israel) for its sin. In the middle of the punishment appears this promise of hope. Scholars debate whether it speaks of a nearby deliverance, the restoration of Israel, or the final resurrection. The apostle Paul uses similar words in 1 Corinthians 15:55 when speaking of victory over death.

Today, when you feel fear about death, a loss, or your own failures, remember that God has the last word. Trust his promise and live with hope.
exp.11:4:
It says that Jacob wrestled with an angel and came out on top, but that he did it weeping and pleading. "Prevailed" means that he achieved what he was seeking. The verse says he wept and sought his favor. It adds that God found him at Bethel, and that there God spoke with us, that is, with the people descended from Jacob.

Hosea, a prophet of the northern kingdom (Israel), speaks in God's name. God has a legal dispute with Judah and with Israel because of their unfaithfulness. Hosea recalls the story of Jacob, who wrestled with God (Genesis 32) and found God at Bethel (Genesis 28 and 35). Some understand Jacob's strength to be his persistence in prayer; others see in it a warning against trusting one's own strength.

God is not impressed by strength, but by a humble heart that weeps and seeks. Today you can draw near to Him with sincerity, without pretending, and ask Him with confidence.
exp.7:8:
Here the verse says that Israel, called Ephraim after its main tribe, went to seek help from Assyria. It is compared to a wild donkey, an untamed animal that roams on its own, stubborn and independent. The phrase "hired lovers" is an image: Ephraim paid gifts and tribute to foreign nations, like someone who pays for affection instead of trusting in their God. Assyria is the nation meant.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel sought political security through alliances instead of returning to the Lord. That is why God says they have sown the wind and will reap the whirlwind: their decisions would bring ruin. Scholars often connect this with the payments made to Assyria in the 8th century B.C.

For today: when we are afraid or in need, let us not run first to what seems safe, such as money, influence, or people. Let us first bring everything to God in prayer and ask for his guidance. He never leaves us alone.
exp.5:8:
It says that a group of priests acts like robbers who hide in ambush to attack someone. On the road they commit murder, and they do it by common agreement. The phrase about carrying out a horrible wickedness means that they carry out a terrible evil.

Some scholars believe this refers to real crimes committed near Shechem; others understand it in a more general way. It is not known with certainty.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He accuses Israel of breaking the covenant, and here he points to its religious leaders. Those who should have guided the people toward God were harming them. That is why the text goes on to speak of Israel's spiritual corruption.

For today: those who hold spiritual authority should care for others, not take advantage of them. We can pray for our leaders and examine how we ourselves use any influence we have.
exp.10:6:
This verse says that God's people are stuck to their rebellion, like someone who will not let go. Even though they are called toward the Most High, that is, toward God, no one is willing to lift him up or honor him. The verse's comment on the word for "bent" is that it means clinging or holding fast, and its comment on the word for "exalt" is that it means praising and placing God in the highest place.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim. First he recalls his fatherly love, but the people rejected him, and so he announces the consequences under Assyria. Yet soon his heart is moved, and he decides not to destroy them completely.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is something we are holding on to even though God calls us to let it go. Responding quickly to his voice, with humility and praise, opens the door to his mercy, which keeps seeking us.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that the hearts of Israel's leaders burned like an oven, full of crooked plans. The baker sleeps through the night while the oven still holds its coals, and in the morning the flame flares up again. In the same way, their evil plans seemed calm, but they stayed ready to catch fire.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. He denounces the unfaithfulness and conspiracies of the court. The verses that follow say that several kings fell. Some think the image describes a palace plot, though the details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: anger, envy, or ambition that we keep quiet does not disappear; it only waits for a spark. Today we can bring those hidden desires before God, ask him for a clean heart, and seek peace before something catches fire.
exp.13:6:
They who return to God will live again under his shadow and his protection. They will be brought back to life, "vivificados como trigo," that is, they will come back to life and bear fruit like grain that grows. They will flourish like the vine, and their fragrance will be like the wine of Lebanon, a region famous for its scents and its beauty. "Under his shadow" may refer to the shadow of God or to that of the restored people; scholars understand it in different ways.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned away from Him through idolatry and disobedience, but at the end of the book God promises to heal, forgive, and restore those who repent. The images of plants show new life after a time of dryness.

For today: if you feel dry or far from God, do not think that all is lost. Return to Him with sincerity, leave behind what pulls you away, and trust that His forgiveness can give you life and fruit again.
exp.13:1:
Hosea invites the people to return to God, but not empty-handed: "take words with you," that is, a sincere prayer. He teaches them what to say: "Take away all iniquity" (forgive every sin) and "receive us graciously" (accept the good we offer). "The calves of our lips" means offering praise and thanksgiving in place of animals.

The prophet Hosea speaks to the kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from God through idols and alliances with powers such as Assyria. After warning them of judgment, God himself opens a way back and even gives them the words to ask for forgiveness. The verses that follow show repentance: ceasing to trust in Assyria, in horses, and in idols, and trusting in God.

For today: when you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you feel perfect. Go to him with simple, honest words, ask for forgiveness, and trust in his mercy.
exp.2:3:
It says that Israel would spend a long time without its political and religious supports: without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an image (a pillar or sacred stone, which could be used in true or false worship), without an ephod (the priest's garment, linked to seeking God's guidance) and without teraphim (household idols). It is a time of emptiness and of being left without what was familiar.

God speaks through Hosea. The prophet bought his wife Gomer and kept her apart for a time in order to restore her. That illustrates how God deals with Israel, who had been unfaithful to him. Interpreters explain the "many days" in several ways, but the text that follows shows that the goal is the return to God.

For today: sometimes God allows you to lose things you trusted in, to teach you to seek Him alone. If you go through a time of emptiness, do not waste it: draw near to God with sincerity.
exp.3:9:
It says the people will eat, yet they will remain hungry; they will practice sexual immorality, yet they will not have more children. "Being satisfied" means being full and content, and "increasing" means multiplying. The reason is clear: they stopped paying attention to the Lord, that is, they stopped listening to him and obeying him.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel. He accuses the priests and the people of living in wickedness and of profiting from the people's sin. Many understand the "sexual immorality" both literally and spiritually, because of the idolatry mentioned afterward. God warns that their actions will have consequences.

When we push God away from the center of life, we may have things and pleasures, yet we remain empty. Today we can ask ourselves what we are looking for to fill ourselves, and return to listening to God with humility.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the grain and the wine, which the people expected from their harvests, will no longer feed them. The threshing floor is the place where grain is beaten out, and the winepress is where grapes are trodden. The new wine is the fresh juice of the grape, and "shall fail" means that it will run out or not bear fruit.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to Israel. Some believe the people celebrated harvest festivals, attributing the abundance to false gods, and for this reason God calls this "whoredom," that is, being unfaithful to him. For this reason he warns them that their harvests will fail, as a consequence of their unfaithfulness.

For today: everything good we have comes from God, not only from our own effort. We can ask ourselves whether we are trusting in money or work more than in Him, and thank Him sincerely.
exp.3:5:
It says that God's people were "destroyed," that is, cut down like a tree, because they lacked knowledge. Here "knowledge" means knowledge of God and of his law. The priests rejected it, that is, they turned it away on purpose. That is why God says he will "reject you from the priesthood" and that, since they forgot his law, he too will "forget your children."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing Israel, the northern kingdom. He accuses especially the priests, who were supposed to teach the law to the people and did not. Through that neglect, everyone went astray. Some scholars think the words "I will reject you" refer to the priests, and others to the whole people.

For today: do not neglect to know God's Word. Set aside time regularly to read it, and if you teach others, do so faithfully, because a lack of knowledge also affects the family.
exp.1:2:
It says that God warns what he would do if she does not give up her unfaithfulness: he would strip her of everything, leave her naked as on the day she was born, and her life would become like a wilderness, like dry land, dying of thirst. "Strip" means to take away everything one has. "Return" means to go back to an earlier state. "Plead" means to bring a formal complaint or charge.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who looks for other lovers, that is, the idols, and credits them with the bread, the water, and the wool, when all of it comes from God. The names Lo-ammi ("not my people") and Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied") call the children to plead with their mother. The warning aims to make her react and return.

For today: ask yourself where you really expect your security and your provision to come from. Thank God for what you have, and do not place your trust in things that cannot sustain you.
exp.7:13:
Israel has forgotten the one who made him, and who formed him as a nation. Instead of trusting in God, he has built temples (probably for idols, or for a religion shaped to suit his own convenience), and Judah has filled the land with fortified cities. God answers that he will send fire upon those cities, and it will consume their palaces. "Maker" means Creator; "I will send" is the sense of the verb rendered as "I will send."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom of Israel and also Judah. The people had God's law, but they treated it as something foreign. Their religion was only ritual, and they trusted in political and military security. God calls them to account for abandoning their relationship with him.

For today: examine where you place your security. Houses, savings, work, or religious activities can become a substitute for God. Set aside time each day to remember that he is your Creator and to obey him sincerely.
exp.5:5:
It tells us that God takes more pleasure in faithful, compassionate love (mercy) than in animal sacrifices. It also says he prefers that we truly know him, more than whole burnt offerings placed completely on the altar.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Ephraim and Judah claimed to love God, but their faithfulness lasted as briefly as the morning cloud or the dew, which soon vanish. They kept the rituals, but they broke the covenant, as the following verse shows.

Today we can examine whether our faith is only religious habit or whether it shows in how we treat others. This week, practice a specific act of mercy toward someone and seek to know God better through his Word.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that the LORD has a case, that is, an accusation or a legal dispute, against Judah. He is going to call Jacob to account, which here means asking for an account of his conduct. "According to his ways" means according to his way of living. The next phrase means that God will repay them according to what they have done.

The prophet Hosea, a messenger of God, speaks in a time of deceit and political alliances with Assyria and Egypt. Some think Judah receives a warning even though it was praised earlier; others see a reference to the whole nation. The text allows both readings.

For today: God sees our way of living, not only what we say. Today you can examine your decisions and return to Him with sincerity, trusting in His mercy.
exp.9:14:
It says that what happened at Bethel, the place where Israel worshiped idols, will turn back on the people because of their great wickedness. "Bethel" is the place Bethel, and the phrase "great wickedness" means a very great evil. "In a morning" suggests that the judgment will come suddenly, and "utterly cut off" means that the king of Israel will be completely removed.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people trusted in their armies and in their own way, and they worshiped calves at Bethel. Scholars are not completely certain who Shalman was or where and when the battle of Beth-arbel took place, and several ideas have been proposed. The message is clear: God warns of judgment for their idolatry and injustice.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in: our money, our strength, or our plans, or God. It is better to turn back to Him now, with humility, before we reap the bitter fruit of living far from Him.
exp.2:4:
Afterward, Hosea says, after a long time without a king or proper worship, the people of Israel will return. They will seek the Lord their God and David their king. The word "fear" here means coming near with reverence and awe, not with terror, and "his goodness" refers to the good that God gives. "In the latter days" points to a future time, and it is understood in different ways.

Hosea is the prophet speaking. God had told him to love an unfaithful woman, as a picture of how Israel had been unfaithful to God. The verse before shows a time of waiting and discipline. Many Christians see in "David their king" a reference to Christ, a descendant of David, though others understand it in other ways.

Even when we have drifted away, God leaves the door open to return. If today you feel far from Him, seek Him sincerely and trust in His goodness.
exp.7:5:
It says the calf of Samaria did not come from God, but from the hands of an Israelite craftsman. So it is not a god, only a manufactured object. "Craftsman" means a maker who works with his hands, and the calf is a young bull made as an idol. God announces that this idol will be broken to pieces.

The one speaking is God, through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel, whose capital was Samaria. The people had set up kings without consulting God and had made idols from their silver and gold. Scholars usually understand the calf as a cult idol in Samaria, although some debate the details of how it was used. God shows them the absurdity of worshiping something they made themselves.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we have made, such as money, success, or image, and to which we give the place of God. What we make cannot save us. Let us return to the true God, who truly sustains us.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that Ephraim, which is another name for the northern kingdom of Israel, has given itself completely to idols. That is why God says "let him alone", meaning "do not keep pressing him, leave him as he is." "Given to" means devoted or attached to something.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just warned Judah not to imitate the unfaithfulness of Israel. Israel has been stubborn, like a rebellious cow that will not be led. There are different views on the tone of "let him alone": some see it as a severe judgment, others as a painful warning that lets him suffer the consequences of his own choice.

For today: examine what things are taking the place of God in your heart. If you have hardened your heart, do not wait any longer. Return to Him today, while you can still hear His voice.
exp.7:3:
It says that the people of Israel set up kings and rulers without consulting God or seeking his approval. Moreover, they made idols out of their silver and gold, and this would lead them to their own ruin. The words "cut off" in the verse mean cut off or destroyed, and "princes" are chiefs or rulers.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. They claimed to know him, yet they lived apart from him. That is why God shows them that their politics and their religion did not come from obedience. Scholars debate exactly which kings are meant, but the central idea is clear: they acted on their own.

For today: before making important decisions, such as work, family, or money, ask God and seek his guidance in the Bible. It is also wise to examine where we place our resources, so that they do not become idols that end up harming us.
exp.0:4:
It says that God himself will break the military power of Israel, the northern kingdom. The bow was the main weapon of war, so it stands for their strength and their security. "It shall come to pass" means that it will happen, and "at that day" points to a moment of judgment that was drawing near. The place is the valley of Jezreel, a plain where many battles were fought.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He asks him to give his son the name Jezreel, a name carrying a warning. Jezreel recalled the blood shed in the time of Jehu, and God announces that he will call them to account. Israel trusted in its army and its alliances, not in God. Scholars debate exactly which events the "blood of Jezreel" refers to, but the central message is clear: judgment will come.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether money, work or plans. All of that can fail, but God does not.
exp.4:9:
The leaders of Judah are said to have acted like those who move the boundary markers of a piece of land in order to take land that belongs to someone else. The stones that marked the limits of each property are the ones in view here. For this reason God announces that he will pour out his anger on them with force, as water is poured out.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. The people had turned away from him, and the northern kingdom (Ephraim) was in sin. Now Judah, the southern kingdom, is also accused of injustice and of breaking what God had established. The law forbade moving boundary markers (Deuteronomy 19:14). Interpreters differ on whether Hosea is speaking of literal theft of land or using the image to speak of crossing the limits of God's law in general.

Today, God sees how we use power. Ask yourself: is there some boundary of honesty that I am moving to my own advantage? Seek to live with justice and respect, even when no one sees you.
exp.6:14:
God says that He "girded" Israel, that is, clothed them with strength and prepared them, and that He "strengthened their arms," meaning He gave them power and victory. Even so, they "imagined mischief" against Him: they planned evil and turned away from their God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). He complains like a wounded father: He had rescued and strengthened them, yet they sought help from other nations and cried out only for grain and wine, not for Him.

For today: let us recognize that all strength, health, and ability come from God. Instead of using His gifts to live far from Him, let us give Him thanks today and seek Him sincerely, not only when we need something.
exp.0:8:
God tells Hosea to name his third child Lo-ammi, which means "not my people." It is a harsh message: the people of Israel have turned away from God, and He declares that He no longer acknowledges them as His own. "You" here means "you all."

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel, which lived in idolatry and unfaithfulness. The names of the prophet's children were living signs of that judgment. Yet the verses that follow announce hope: one day they will be called "children of the living God." Judgment is not the final word.

For today: God takes our faithfulness seriously, but His desire is to restore us. If you have wandered away from Him, do not remain in guilt; return to Him with confidence, for His mercy is greater than your failure.
exp.3:12:
It says that the people of Israel offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, on the tops of the mountains and the hills, under trees that gave pleasant shade: oaks, poplars and elms. The word "burned" in the verse means they burned incense. "Commit whoredom" and "commit adultery" speak of sexual unfaithfulness. For this reason, God says, their daughters and their daughters-in-law would fall into that same behavior.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. His people had abandoned Jehovah to worship idols, and that worship was often mixed with sexual practices. Scholars explain in various ways how literal this was, but the text links it with spiritual unfaithfulness. The consequences reach the families.

For today: let us take care with what we worship and with what we do for comfort. What seems pleasant, like a good shade, can draw us away from God and affect our children. Let us live faithfully to God at home.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the introduction to the book. It says that what follows is "the word of the Lord," meaning a message that God himself gave to Hosea, the son of Beeri. The phrase "came unto Hosea" means that the word came to Hosea. Then it names the kings of Judah (Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah) and Jeroboam, king of Israel, to place the message in time.

The one speaking is the author of the book, who presents Hosea as a prophet. We know nothing more about Beeri. The kings mentioned indicate that Hosea ministered over many years, in a time of instability and idolatry in Israel, the northern kingdom. Some scholars note that Jeroboam, the son of Joash, is the only king of Israel named, and they explain this in different ways.

For today: God speaks in real history, not in a vacuum. Before you offer your own opinion, ask him to speak to you through his Word, and obey it even when the moment is difficult.
exp.7:1:
Hosea 8:2 says that when danger comes, Israel will cry out to God and say, "My God, we know thee." It is a cry for help that sounds very sure of itself.

The verse is spoken by God through the prophet Hosea. He has just announced that an enemy will come like an eagle against his house, because the people broke the covenant and rebelled against his law. That is why this cry is not sincere: they say they know him, but their lives contradict it. Later in the chapter we see that they had set up kings without consulting him and made idols.

For today: it is not enough to say "I know God" when problems arrive. Really knowing him shows in obeying him every day, not only in asking him for help during a crisis. Today you can ask yourself: does my life show what my mouth says?
exp.9:8:
God reminds Israel that its sin goes back a long way, to the days of Gibeah. He says that "there they stood," meaning they kept on in the same wickedness without changing. The last phrase is hard: it can mean that the battle did not overtake them back then, or that it will overtake them now.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, called Israel or Ephraim. Gibeah recalls a terrible episode of wickedness and violence, told in Judges 19 to 21. God uses that memory to show that the people are repeating old sins, and for that reason judgment is coming.

For today: let us not take lightly the repeated sins we have carried for years. Today we can acknowledge before God an old habit, ask him for forgiveness, and seek help to change, trusting in his mercy.
exp.4:2:
God knows Ephraim perfectly, since Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, and so the verse names all of Israel after it. Nothing about Israel is hidden from him. The word "whoredom" here speaks of spiritual unfaithfulness: leaving God to follow other gods. "Defiled" means stained, made unclean.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Earlier, God had accused the priests and the king of having been a snare and a net, that is, of having trapped the people and led them astray, in places like Mizpah and Tabor. God does not overlook what is happening; that is why judgment is coming, and the people no longer think of returning to him.

For today: God sees even what we try to hide. That is frightening, but it also invites us to return to him with sincerity, without excuses or appearances, trusting that the one who knows us can also forgive us.
exp.9:0:
Israel is compared here to a large vine full of leaves. But that vine bore fruit "for itself," that is, for its own benefit. The more it prospered, the more altars it built for its idols. The "images" refers to pillars or sacred stones used in pagan worship. The better the land did, the more the people gave themselves over to idolatry.

Here the prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, Israel, shortly before its fall. God denounces that the people used their blessings to worship idols and not Him. The following verse says that their heart was divided and that God would tear down those altars.

For today: blessings should draw us closer to God, not push us away. Ask yourself whether, when things go well for you, your gratitude and your service to God grow, or whether you begin to trust more in your achievements and possessions.
exp.10:3:
God says he led Israel with human cords, that is, with gentle and close care, with cords of love. He is compared to someone who loosens the yoke from the animal's jaw so that it can eat with more ease, and then brings the food close to it.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He remembers how he cared for Israel, here called Ephraim, like a little child he taught to walk. Yet the people turned away and worshiped the Baals. For this reason the warning of judgment follows. Some understand the loosened yoke as an image of freedom; the general meaning is God's tender care.

For today: think of some help you have received that you did not recognize as God's care. Thank him today and respond with trusting obedience, without hardening your heart.
exp.12:11:
It says that the wickedness of Ephraim is "bound up", that is, tied tight like a securely closed bundle, and that his sin is "hid", meaning recorded and kept in reserve. God has not forgotten it. Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, Israel.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He accuses Israel of having rejected his care and of having trusted in human kings. Their guilt does not vanish on its own, and judgment will come in its time. Even so, shortly afterward, the same chapter speaks of redemption and of victory over death.

For today: we cannot hide our sins or pretend they are already past. The wisest course is to bring them to God with sincerity and repentance, trusting that He forgives and sets free whoever returns to Him.
exp.10:11:
Hosea 11:12 says, in the King James Version: "Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the saints." The word "compasseth" means surrounded. Ephraim and Israel (the northern kingdom) filled their dealings with God with falsehood. Judah, for now, still walks with God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. He has just promised to restore his people, but he shows that they answered him with hypocrisy and lies. The last part is understood in several ways. Some believe it praises Judah, and others that it also corrects it.

For today: God looks for sincerity, not just religious words. Today you can pray openly, acknowledge your failures before him, and ask him for a faithful heart.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that Gilead was a city full of people who practiced evil, and that it was stained with blood. "Workers of iniquity" are those who do wrong, and "polluted with blood" speaks of violence and unjust killings.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea and accuses the people of the northern kingdom, Israel. Earlier he said that he wanted mercy and the knowledge of him, not only offerings. Scholars are not sure which exact event is meant here, nor which city in the region of Gilead is in view. But the message is clear: their religion was not changing their conduct.

For today: going to church or keeping rituals is not enough. Ask God that your faith show in how you treat others, with justice, respect, and mercy.
exp.4:14:
God says that he will withdraw and return to his place, that is, he will step away from them, until they acknowledge their guilt and truly seek him. The phrase "I will go and return" means that he will go away and come back, and "seek me early" means that they will look for him eagerly, early, urgently, when they are in trouble.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom (Ephraim) and also to Judah. They trusted in Assyria and not in God, and he warns them that no human king will be able to heal them. His withdrawal works as discipline, with the hope of leading them to repentance. Some understand this as the exile that would come; the text gives no further details.

For today: when you feel that God is silent or things are becoming difficult, do not rush first to other ways out. Examine your heart, acknowledge whatever needs to be acknowledged, and seek him with sincerity. He receives those who return to him.
exp.6:13:
