God says that his people did not truly seek him. They wailed and cried out while lying on their beds, but it was not a sincere cry. They gathered together only for grain and new wine, that is, for food and drink. The word "howled" describes moaning like an animal, and "assemble themselves" may refer to gathering to ask for harvests. Meanwhile, they continued to rebel against God.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the kingdom of Israel (also called Ephraim), in the 8th century BC. He accuses them of hypocrisy: they say it with their mouths, but their hearts are far away. Some interpret the gathering as rituals tied to gods of rain and harvest, though the text does not fully make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves why we pray. It is good to ask for bread and provision, but God wants our hearts, not only his gifts. Let us seek today to know him, not only to receive from him.
exp.6:3:
He says that the whole people is unfaithful to God, and that their desire to sin burns like a heated oven. The baker stops stoking the fire while the dough rises, but the embers keep burning. "Adulterers" speaks of physical unfaithfulness and also of leaving God for other gods.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the kingdom of Israel, in the north. He reminds them that he does not forget their wickedness. The leaders and the king rejoice in sin and in lies. Interpreters explain the image in different ways, but nearly all of them see a passion that does not go out and that waits for the moment to break out.

For today: do not believe that an evil desire goes away on its own just because it is quiet. Bring it to God in time, before it grows, and seek help in prayer and from trusted people.
exp.12:15:
Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, is said to be left in ruins because it rebelled against God. "Desolate" means stripped bare and left in ruins. "Fall by the sword" means they will die by the sword. The verse describes the violence of war: the infants will be dashed against the ground, and the pregnant women will be ripped open by the sword.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had abandoned God to follow Baal and to rely on alliances with other nations. Many understand that the punishment came through Assyria, around 722 B.C. These are cruel images that reflect the warfare customs of that time; the text does not say that God takes pleasure in them, but warns of the consequences of stubborn rejection.

For today: God takes sin seriously, but he still offers forgiveness. If something is pulling you away from him, return today with humility, before the consequences grow.
exp.6:10:
Hosea says that Ephraim, that is, the northern kingdom of Israel, was acting like a naive dove with no sense. A frightened dove flies back and forth without any direction. In the same way, the people called for help from Egypt and then ran toward Assyria.

The word "silly" in the verse means foolish, or easy to deceive. The phrase "without heart" means without understanding.

Here God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel was being weakened by foreign nations, but did not realize it. Instead of returning to God, the people sought political alliances with neighboring powers. God warns them that this misplaced trust will bring their downfall, because they had turned away from the One who had redeemed them.

For today: when pressure, worry, or need comes, let us not run from one human solution to another without first seeking God. We may ask for advice and practical help, but our first look should go to Him, who is faithful and secure.
exp.9:4:
This verse says that the people of Samaria will be afraid because of the calves of Beth-aven. The word for these images, the statues of young bulls that they worshiped, is rendered in the verse as "calves." Beth-aven means "house of wickedness" and is used here as a nickname for Bethel. The people and their priests will mourn because their idol, the thing they took pride in, will be taken away or will disappear. The word for being scattered or lost is used in the sense of being carried off and gone.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea to the northern kingdom, Israel. The people had made false alliances and worshiped idols instead of trusting in the LORD. The verses that follow say that the idol will be carried to Assyria as tribute. Some think this refers to a historical event that was close at hand; the text itself gives no further detail.

Whatever we put in place of God, whether money, success or reputation, cannot save us and can leave us weeping. Today, ask yourself: what gives me more security than God does? Give it to Him sincerely.
exp.7:6:
It says that Israel has sown the wind, that is, something empty and useless, and for that reason it will reap the whirlwind, a violent destruction. In addition, the wheat will not come to ear; and if the grain were to yield any flour, foreigners will swallow it up, that is, eat it. A "harvest" is the cereal crop; to "reap" is to gather in the harvest.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressed to the northern kingdom (Israel, also called Ephraim). The people had made idols, such as the calf of Samaria, and sought alliances with nations like Assyria instead of trusting in God. The text announces that those paths would end in loss and foreign rule.

For today: what we sow has consequences. If we place our trust in empty things, such as money, success, or the approval of others, we will reap more emptiness. Today you can sow in what lasts: prayer, honesty, and trust in God.
exp.1:14:
God promises to return to his people their vineyards, that is, the abundance and blessing they had lost. Furthermore, the valley of Achor, which means "trouble," will become a "door of hope." There the people will sing, as in the days of their youth, when they came up out of Egypt.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had been unfaithful, like a wife who runs after other lovers, worshiping the Baals. God corrects her, but he does not abandon her: he leads her into the wilderness to speak to her heart. The valley of Achor recalls Joshua 7, where there was sin and punishment; now God transforms it into hope.

For today: if you are going through a place of pain or failure, do not think it is the end. Return to God with sincerity. He can turn your valleys of trouble into doors of hope and give you back your song.
exp.11:1:
This verse says that Ephraim, that is the northern kingdom of Israel, "feeds on the wind," meaning it chases something that gives no nourishment and bears no fruit. The hot, dry east wind that destroys crops is the thing the wind here stands for. Ephraim multiplies lies and ruin, because it makes deals with Assyria and sends oil to Egypt, probably as payment or a gift to win political support.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, in the eighth century B.C. Israel trusted in alliances with the great powers instead of trusting the Lord. God calls this deceit and disloyalty. Judah appears to be in a better position at that moment, though the following text shows that it too will be called to account.

For today: when anxiety pushes us to seek security in money, influence, or empty promises, it is wise to stop and ask whether these things truly sustain us. Trusting God and asking him for direction is firmer ground than chasing the wind.
exp.3:18:
A strong wind wrapped Israel in its wings and carried her away, like someone being dragged along who cannot resist. The sentence that explains the word for "bound her up" is removed, since that word does not appear in the verse. In the end, the sacrifices they offered to idols will only bring them shame, because they did them no good.

The prophet Hosea speaks, sent by God to the northern kingdom, called Ephraim. The people had given themselves over to idols and immorality, and their leaders sought bribes. Some understand "the wings" as the wings of the wind itself; others see it as a picture of the judgment that would come upon them. In either case, the message is that their rebellion would end in ruin.

For today: examine what you place your trust in. If you seek security in anything other than God, sooner or later it will vanish like the wind. Return to Him with sincerity.
exp.12:6:
It says that God himself, who once cared for Israel, will now appear before them like a lion, and like a leopard that lies in wait beside the road. The word "observe" here means to watch closely, waiting for the right moment. The image is not of a friendly animal, but of a danger close at hand.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing the northern kingdom, Israel. He cared for them in the wilderness and gave them food, but when they were satisfied they became proud and forgot him. The images of wild beasts express judgment for that ingratitude, although the context ends by pointing out that help is found only in God.

For today: when everything is going well for us, it is easy to forget God. Today you can thank him for what you have and ask him for a humble heart, one that does not depend only on comfort.
exp.1:10:
God says he will bring an end to Israel's joy and all its religious celebrations: the yearly feasts, the new moons (the start of each month), and the sabbaths. The solemn feast days were their set holy occasions. Everything that seemed like life and blessing will come to a stop.

The LORD speaks through the prophet Hosea. He compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who goes after the Baals, Canaanite gods, and believes they give her the grain, the wine, and the wool. Because she forgot God, he takes away her blessings so that she will wake up. The feasts continued, but they were mixed with idolatry, so they did not please God. The punishment aims to bring her back to him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our religion is sincere or just a custom. Let us thank God as the true giver of everything, and not trust in money, success, or pleasures. He corrects in order to restore us.
exp.3:6:
It says that the more they grew in number, power and position, the more they sinned against God. The word "increased" speaks of their growth or prosperity. The word "change" means to exchange, and "shame" is disgrace. God promises to change their honor into dishonor.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea, addressing above all the priests of Israel. They had the task of teaching the law, but they forgot it. Some understand the increase to refer to the growth of the priests; others, to the whole nation. In either case, the problem is that their privilege did not draw them closer to God, but pushed them away.

For today: when God gives us more success, influence or responsibility, it is wise to become more humble and more attentive to his Word. Blessings are not an excuse for neglecting God, but a reason to honor him more.
exp.4:7:
The passage says that the alarm of war should be sounded in three cities of Benjamin: Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth-aven. The horn and the trumpet were instruments that signaled danger. The cry "after you, O Benjamin" can be understood as meaning that the enemy is coming up behind Benjamin, or as a battle cry. Scholars interpret it in several ways. The name Beth-aven means "house of wickedness" and probably refers to Bethel, where there was an idol.

God speaks through the prophet Hosea. Israel had turned its back on God through its idolatry, and now judgment would come. The cities named were on the border, and the alarm warns that punishment is near.

For today: God warns us before the consequences arrive. If we notice that something has taken God's place in our hearts, let us not wait until it is too late. Let us return to God today with sincerity, for He welcomes whoever repents.

sum.11: God accuses Ephraim and Israel of lying and deceiving, of making alliances with other nations and of gaining wealth dishonestly, all while claiming they have done nothing wrong. He reminds them of Jacob, who wrestled and sought God, and calls them to return to Him, to practice mercy and justice, and to always wait on Him. If they do not, they will receive the payment for their deeds.
sum.5: Hosea 6 begins with a call to return to the LORD, who wounds but also heals. But God answers that his people's love is as fleeting as the morning dew. He says he desires mercy and the knowledge of God more than sacrifices, and he denounces Israel and Judah for breaking the covenant, for violence, and for immorality.
sum.1: In Hosea 2, God compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who runs after other lovers (Baal) and forgets that God was the one giving her everything. Because of this, God announces punishment and scarcity, but then promises to lead her into the wilderness, speak tenderly to her heart, and restore her. In the end, God betroths her forever, in righteousness and mercy, and says, "You are my people."
sum.4: God accuses the priests, the king, and the people of Israel of idolatry and pride, and announces punishment for Judah as well. Even if they seek him with sacrifices, they will not find him, because their hearts have turned away and they do not know him. God will act like a moth and like a lion until they recognize their sin and seek him in distress.
sum.0: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, and their children are given names that announce judgment: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah ("not pitied"), and Lo-ammi ("not my people"), because Israel has turned away from God. But God promises mercy to Judah and, in the end, to restore his people, calling them "children of the living God."
sum.7: God warns that an enemy will come against Israel because they broke their covenant, set up kings without consulting him, made idols such as the calf of Samaria, and sought alliances with Assyria instead of trusting in him. They sowed the wind and will reap the whirlwind. God rejects their empty sacrifices and announces punishment.
sum.12: God accuses Ephraim (Israel) of forgetting him after receiving prosperity, and of falling into the worship of Baal and the golden calves. Because of this, their reputation will vanish like morning mist, and judgment and destruction will come upon Samaria. Even so, God promises to redeem them from death and the grave, and reminds them that he alone is Savior.
sum.13: The prophet Hosea calls Israel to return to God and ask for forgiveness with sincere words, giving up trust in Assyria, in war horses, and in idols. God promises to heal their rebellion, love them freely, and make them flourish like a lily, an olive tree, and a grapevine. The chapter ends by saying that God's ways are straight: the righteous walk in them, but rebels stumble.
sum.10: God remembers how he loved Israel from the time they were young. He brought them out of Egypt and cared for them tenderly, but the people turned away to other gods and refused to come back to him. Because of this, judgment will come. Yet God's heart is moved, and he decides not to destroy them completely. He promises to bring his children back to their homes.
sum.6: In Hosea 7, God wants to heal Israel, but he uncovers their deceit, their wickedness, and the corruption of their kings and leaders. The people do not cry out to God from the heart; instead, they look for help to Egypt and Assyria, and because of this they will face judgment. God reminds them that he redeemed them and strengthened them, but they rebelled against him.
sum.8: God tells Israel not to rejoice, because it has abandoned him and loved the rewards of idolatry. For this reason it will lose its harvests, be carried off to Egypt and Assyria, and its children will not prosper. The prophets warn, but the people reject them, and God casts them off for not listening to him.
sum.9: Israel, like a lush vine, used its abundance to multiply its altars and idols, and so God will bring judgment: its king will be cut off, the idols will be destroyed, and the people will be taken away to Assyria. But God calls them to sow righteousness and seek Him, because they trusted in their own strength and reaped wickedness.
sum.2: God tells Hosea to love a woman again, even though she has been unfaithful to him, just as God loves Israel even though Israel has turned to other gods. Hosea buys her back and asks her to remain faithful to him for many days. In the same way, Israel will go a long time without a king or worship, but in the end it will return to seek the LORD and his goodness.
sum.3: God accuses Israel because there is no longer any truth, mercy, or knowledge of Him in the land, and lying, theft, adultery, and violence are everywhere. The priests and the people have turned away from the law, sought out idols and vices, and for this reason shame and judgment will come. Judah is warned not to follow that same path.
